title: Nasdaq 100 falls 5.5% as AI market faces reassessment
content:
After a wobble on the tech‑heavy Nasdaq, some AI market observers think a reassessment of the potential value of various businesses may be under way. The world is holding its breath as it waits to find out whether this year’s estimated $US1tn investment in artificial intelligence is resting on a castle made of sand.

title: AI touted to save time is flooding inboxes with low‑quality content, says Gaby Hinsliff
content:
The Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff argues that the government’s promise of AI transforming the state has instead produced a “stream of machine‑generated slop.” She notes that, despite the claim that AI will streamline public services, the reality is that it has flooded inboxes with unwanted emails.

Hinsliff describes her own experience: after a “guilty cull,” her inbox still holds well over 7,000 messages. She likens the accumulation to the Quentin Crisp theory of housework, suggesting that empty inboxes quickly refill. The author points out that email was intended to save hours of meetings, phone calls, and photocopying, but now requires hours of deleting spam that would have otherwise been handled by a phone call.

She concludes that the convenience of reaching the world in seconds comes with the inconvenience of being able to be reached back with a single click, highlighting the unintended costs of the technology she once championed.
summary: The article notes the government claims AI can transform the state, yet the resulting wave of machine‑generated content is overwhelming. Guardian columnist Gaby Hinsliff observes her inbox holds over 7,000 messages, with AI‑driven spam undermining email’s intended time‑saving benefits.

title: Googlebook laptops launch at £999 but suffer software flaws, review says
content:
Google has introduced a new line of laptops called the Googlebook, designed to blend ChromeOS with Android features. The company aims to position these devices as competitors to Windows and macOS machines, offering advanced integration with Android phones and core Google services. In a review, the author notes that while the hardware is strong, software flaws detract from the overall experience.

The author tested two Googlebooks, noting that the devices are built by established PC manufacturers such as Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo. The price point for the entry‑level model starts at £999, equivalent to €1,099, $899, or A$2,299, which is significantly higher than the £160 price range typically associated with Chromebooks.

Compared to the budget‑friendly Chromebooks that have dominated the low‑cost laptop market for years, the Googlebook takes a premium approach. The review questions whether the new laptops can truly rival the performance and value offered by devices like the MacBook Air or the Surface Laptop.
summary: Google’s new laptops, called Googlebooks, combine ChromeOS with Android, are made by Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, and start at £999 (€1,099/$899/A$2,299). A review found the devices have strong hardware but are let down by software flaws, making them underbaked compared with competitors.

content:

The outage has highlighted the vulnerability of fintech platforms that rely on cloud infrastructure for day‑to‑day operations.

In other economic news, Britain’s unemployment rate fell unexpectedly to 4.7% this morning, prompting a rally in the pound. Sterling gained half a cent against the US dollar, trading at $1.3352, as the City welcomed the data that employment rose in the last quarter. The market reacted quickly, with traders scrambling to adjust exposure to the currency.

The labour market remains relatively flat overall, with resilience noted amid global headwinds. However, underlying challenges persist: about one million young people are not in education, employment or training, and overall employment is more than two million short of the Government’s 80 % target. The government has suggested that reforms to the benefit system are needed to provide active help and to make it easier for employers to create jobs.
summary: Google Cloud experienced a major outage in its London region. Revolut customers reported service disruptions as a result.

content:

title: Study finds moon's radius shrank about 148 feet based on 10,000 surface cracks
content:
Scientists have determined that the Moon is slowly shrinking, a conclusion reached through a detailed analysis of images taken by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC). In the new study, researchers identified more than 10,000 young faults—cracks that have formed in the last several hundred million years—across the lunar surface. By cataloguing these features, the team was able to calculate how much the Moon’s radius has decreased over time.

The study estimates that the Moon’s radius has contracted by about 148 feet (45 meters) over the past 400 to 800 million years. Lead author Thomas Watters, a geologist and scientist emeritus at the Center for Earth and Planetary Studies at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum, noted that the number of young faults revealed in the LROC images far exceeds his expectations. He added that as the Moon’s interior continues to cool and contract, the growth of existing faults and the formation of new ones is likely to continue.

The faults mapped in the study include lobate scarps—long, curved structures that form when the Moon’s surface contracts, cracks, and is pushed upward—and small mare ridges, narrow “wrinkles” found on the dark plains. Unlike Earth, which has about 15 major tectonic plates, the Moon is a single‑plate body; its outer shell is a single piece broken only by faults created by contraction.

By mapping thousands of these features, the researchers pieced together aspects of lunar history. They found that some regions of the Moon contain many more faults than others, and that areas with fewer cracks have thicker crust. This suggests that the thicker crust in those regions has been more stable, and that many of the widespread cracks were created later in the Moon’s history, after its early, thicker crust had insulated the interior and slowed cooling.

The findings were published on Oct. 14 in The Planetary Science Journal.
summary: Scientists analyzing Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera images identified over 10,000 young faults on the Moon’s surface. From these features they estimate the Moon’s radius has decreased by about 148 feet (45 meters) over the past 400 to 800 million years.

title: Europe's ExoMars orbiter and Schiaparelli lander arrive at Mars on Oct. 19, 2016
content:
On October 19, 2016, the European Space Agency’s ExoMars 2016 mission arrived at Mars, comprising the Trace Gas Orbiter and the Schiaparelli lander. Launched in March 2016, the spacecraft traveled together before separating on October 16, three days prior to the orbiter entering orbit. The mission was designed to test landing techniques for a future rover and deliver an orbiter to study the Martian atmosphere. Ultimately, the mission was described by ESA officials as "96% successful" due to the loss of the lander.

While the Trace Gas Orbiter successfully entered orbit, the Schiaparelli lander crashed during its descent. It stopped communicating with Earth one minute before its planned landing. Photos from NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter later revealed what appeared to be the crash site and a jettisoned parachute nearby. Officials suspect that a data glitch prevented Schiaparelli from firing its descent thrusters, which were necessary to slow the craft for a safe landing.

The Trace Gas Orbiter remains functional and continues to circle Mars, searching for methane and other gases that could indicate biological activity. The failure of Schiaparelli, combined with the loss of the Russian Proton rocket after ESA severed its partnership with Russia over the war in Ukraine, delayed the ExoMars 2018 mission. This mission includes the Mars rover Rosalind Franklin and is now expected to launch no earlier than 2028, with a landing on Mars anticipated in 2030.

The article also notes that on October 19, 2026, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency attempted to launch the Martian Moons eXploration mission, known as MMX. This mission aims to land a probe on the Mars moon Phobos and return samples to Earth.
summary: On Oct. 19, 2016, the European Space Agency's ExoMars mission arrived at Mars!

title: Lego X‑Files Set Brings 90s Sci‑Fi Nostalgia to Fans
content: Millennials get a lot of flak for being overly nostalgic, but I don't think that's fair. When the modern-day world has nothing to offer us but AI slop, shrinkflation and a sad acceptance that we can't be bothered to do anything about global warming. It's easy to see why we yearn for the days of Pogs, the Backstreet Boys, and Saved by the Bell. One area that we definitely had it good in the 90s was sci-fi, when legendary shows like Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stargate SG-1, and — of course — The X-Files ruled our TV screens long before the age of streaming services. You can relive those glory days of alien conspiracies, spooky happenings and cell phones the size of a brick with the Lego Ideas The X-Files set. This 1478 piece set is essentially two dioramas crammed into a single display piece. The top of the model depicts a spinning UFO floating above one of those iconic coniferous forests that dominated 90s sci-fi. Why? Because — thanks to some generous tax credits — it was cheaper to shoot in Vancouver, so that's where they all flocked. Disney Plus / Hulu bundle: was $12.99 now $11.99 Catch Mulder and Scully in every season of The X-Files on Hulu, which is available bundled with Disney+ for only $11.99/month for the first six months, then increasing to $12.99/month. View Deal Mulder and Scully closing in on our "Grey" alien friend in the woods. (Image credit: Future (Ian Stokes)) Beneath the woodland scene, though, is the real star of the show: Mulder's office, squirrelled away in the basement of the FBI's J. Edgar Hoover Building in Washington, D. C. This dingy little office is where Scully meets "Spooky Mulder", kicking off a glorious sci-fi odyssey that would last for eleven seasons (and two movies). Mulder's dingy little base of operations has been stunningly recreated here, with both overt references and subtle nods that X-Files fans will appreciate. The iconic "I want to believe" poster adorns the wall, alongside photographs of crop circles and a newspaper clipping from a paper called "The Lone Brickman" — a nice nod to " The Lone Gunmen ". There's even an actual X-File sitting on the desk, and a cute Lego spoof of the "Face on Mars", with a photo on the wall that shows a Lego head on the moon. The X-Files Complete Boxset: $160 Prefer to actually own your media? Make your way through this X-Files Complete Boxset on DVD. Just bear in mind that you will need a region-free DVD player to watch it with. The iconic "I Want To Believe" poster. Future (Ian Stokes) Newspaper clippings were a staple of the X-Files office. Future (Ian Stokes) The show's legendary tagline is proudly displayed on the front. Future (Ian Stokes) X(Files) marks the spot. Future (Ian Stokes) It's been a hot minute since I watched The X-Files (that DVD box set beside my TV is calling to me), but even so, I had a blast building my way down memory lane, remembering episodes as I assembled the diorama. I love the little touches, like the display cabinets filled with artifacts, the VHS tapes scattered around the office and the black oil spillage on the floor. As with most Lego sets, the minifigures are half the joy. You get Mulder and Scully, obviously, with the dynamic duo of FBI agents both rocking flashlights (no smartphones with built-in lights back in the 90s). Mulder is wearing dark blue, while Scully is rocking an orangey brown suit, with both of them sporting an FBI badge. Outside of the principal pair, you also get Skinner, Mr X, and the Cigarette Smoking Man. Mulder's partner-turned-nemesis Alex Krycek also gets a suitably devious-looking minifig. It's the gloves, they just make him look like a bad man (which, to be fair, he is). Finally, to ramp up the paranormal scale, we also get a pair of monster minifigs: a grey alien and Flukeman minifigures. The grey alien was a must-have, especially given the UFO floating atop this display piece, but the one-off monster of the week, Flukeman, felt like a weird choice. Agents Mulder and Scully, FBI. Future (Ian Stokes) Assistant Director Skinner, Mr X, and the Cigarette Smoking Man in Mulder's Office. Future (Ian Stokes) Also, this John Doggett erasure will not stand. Sure, he could never replace Mulder, but Robert Patrick's seasons eight and nine run was excellent and he deserved a spot here. And while I'm voicing minor gripes, the usual Lego FOMO tricks were in force with this set; if you pre-ordered, you got an exclusive gift set — Scully's Lab — free of charge. This extra little diorama isn't necessary, but it does feel like the collection is incomplete without it and it's not for sale separately, so you'll have to try your luck with eBay scalpers if you want it. Speaking of Scully, Gillian Anderson has stated that after season 11 wrapped in 2018, she was done with the role. That wasn't entirely accurate, though, as she donned the lab gloves one more time for the Lego X-Files set advert. It's a short bit of fan service, but a nice touch, and, once again, it sparks those 90s neurons. All these delicious Member Berries come at a price, though, and that's the price. This blast from the past will set you back $199 (£179 in the UK). That's no small chunk of change. But then again, anyone who wants this set is in their thirties or forties and can probably afford that outlay for the nostalgia trip. And look at it this way: when The X-Files debuted back in 1993, the price would only have been about $86. I had a great time building the Lego X-Files set and if you're a fan of the series, you will too. Nostalgia often feels like a cheat code to our hearts, but there's nothing wrong with that. We deserve to remember the good times and the truth is that The X-Files was about as good as it ever got for sci-fi fans. You can buy the Lego X-Files set now, available for $199/£179 from the Lego store.
summary: The 1478‑piece Lego X‑Files set recreates a UFO‑hovering forest and Mulder’s basement office and includes minifigures of Mulder, Scully, Skinner, Mr X, the Cigarette Smoking Man, Alex Krycek, a grey alien and Flukeman. Pre‑orders receive a free Scully’s Lab diorama, and the set is priced at $199 and sold through the Lego store.

title: A Zack Snyder DC Universe might not have been such a bad thing, after all
content: After Joss Whedon’s arrival, back in the news with comments from Ben Affleck, the franchise lost a sense of earnest passion that could have sustained a weary DCEU Nine years after superhero epic Justice League arrived in cinemas, there ought to be very little left to say about how it all went wrong. Zack Snyder shot the film, Joss Whedon substantially rewrote and reshot it, and audiences eventually got to see both men’s versions. Any debate over their relative merits long ago disappeared. Whedon is pretty much cancelled; Snyder has reinvented himself as the writer-director of extremely average ersatz Star Wars movies for Netflix, and an entirely new DC universe is under way that has very little to do with either of them. To a greater or lesser extent, the world has moved on. But Ben Affleck’s latest comments raise an uncomfortable question about whether Snyder’s departure was ever presented honestly. Speaking to Josh Horowitz on the Happy Sad Confused podcast, Affleck, who played Batman, described the Justice League reshoots as the lowest point of his career, but reserved his strongest criticism for the circumstances of Snyder’s departure. The director stepped away in May 2017, two months after his daughter Autumn killed herself, aged 20, with the public explanation that he needed to be with his family. Affleck, however, alleged that studio Warner Bros had used the tragedy to justify replacing him. “The way in which that was, I thought, used as an excuse was one of the shittiest things I’ve ever seen,” Affleck said. “It was so gross.”
summary: A Zack Snyder DC Universe might not have been such a bad thing, after all.

title: Ed Sanders: 87‑year‑old counterculture icon who tried to topple the Pentagon
content: He gave Jimi Hendrix his gear, freaked out Frank Sinatra, inspired Norman Mailer – and tried to topple the American war machine. As a documentary about his band the Fugs comes out, the 87-year-old gives a rare interview “Charles Manson once wrote me a letter saying, ‘If I was as powerful as you claim then you wouldn’t be here,’” Ed Sanders tells me over a video call, savouring the menace in that sentence. Sanders is an American maverick; a musician, poet, activist, journalist and author whose greatest hit remains his bestselling 1971 book The Family, in which he chronicled the lives, crimes and trials of Manson and his followers. Sanders was well placed to report on crazed hippies, having played a pivotal role in launching the US counterculture – though he very much espoused peace, love and consciousness-raising, rather than Manson’s apocalyptic worldview.
summary: Ed Sanders: 87‑year‑old counterculture icon who tried to topple the Pentagon.

title: Review: Life Out of Order fails to recapture Niffenegger's original spark
content: More than two decades on, the passion that ignited Niffenegger’s debut has all but evaporated from this confused follow-up I run a reading workshop which begins with a little shelf assessment. Participants bring a stack of books that have shaped who they are: childhood treasures; new revelations; comfort reads. Books they once cherished but have now outgrown. The usual suspect in that category is Audrey Niffenegger’s 2003 novel The Time Traveler’s Wife. Once smitten, readers now find that time-warped romance cruel. What felt like destiny now feels like a cage. As they explain, I’m always struck by the same thought: Wasn’t it always cruel? Wasn’t that the point? Henry DeTamble and Clare Abshire are a couple caught in a causal loop. The irresolvable question is where that loop starts: does a bright young art student fall in love with a junior librarian, or does a time-travelling man groom a child to become his future wife? If the answer is both – and it has to be – what are we to make of their marriage? Can you truly choose someone if you believe the choice is already made?
summary: The reviewer notes that the passion that ignited Niffenegger’s debut has all but evaporated from this confused follow‑up. They describe how readers who once cherished The Time Traveler’s Wife now find its time‑warped romance cruel.

title: With nine new recordings of Mahler’s epic Resurrection Symphony this year alone, which rises above the rest?
content: The second – the ‘Resurrection’ – was the first Mahler symphony ever to be recorded, and it is still today an essential work in any conductor’s catalogue. But with hundreds of recordings, from Ormandy to Bernstein and Rattle, which does our reviewer recommend? Is it something in the water? Or is it simply that triumph over adversity sells in today’s uncertain world? Whatever the reason, Mahler’s Resurrection Symphony has already received four major UK performances this year: a season finale for the BBC Philharmonic in Manchester, a season opener for both the City of Birmingham Symphony Orchestra and the London Symphony Orchestra, and an 80th season celebratory concert for the Philharmonia Orchestra in London. Next month the London City Orchestra perform it in Croydon’s Fairfield Halls. On disc, the field of Mahler 2s is even more crowded. Apple Music Classical currently throws up 222 listings; Presto Music ’s search engine returns 260 results, many of them complete recordings to download or buy on CD or vinyl (some of these, of course, are reissues of recognised classic accounts).
summary: The second – the ‘Resurrection’ – was the first Mahler symphony ever to be recorded, and it is still today an essential work in any conductor’s catalogue. But with hundreds of recordings, from Ormandy to Bernstein and Rattle, which does our reviewer recommend?
author: Guardian Culture

title: Linda Cardellini Talks Horror Role as Pamela Voorhees in Friday the 13th Prequel
content: She got to torment Don Draper in Mad Men and has just won an Emmy for DTF St Louis. But nothing prepared the star for all the gore as she switched to horror with the Friday the 13th prequel ‘The first time I had the tooth in my hand,” says Linda Cardellini, “I thought, ‘Oh my God, this is what I’m doing.’” The star of Freaks and Geeks, ER, Dead to Me, Mad Men and DTF St Louis (for which she recently won an Emmy) is talking about her pivot towards full-blown horror. In Crystal Lake, the prequel to the Friday the 13th movies, Cardellini plays Pamela Voorhees, the original slasher of the 1980 film. The tooth, by the way, is human and gets embedded in Pam’s knuckle – until she yanks it out with a gruesome, revolting slurping sound. Casual filmgoers may associate Friday the 13th with Jason, the hockey-mask-wearing serial killer. But aficionados will know that Pam, Jason’s mother, is the villain of the first movie. “He didn’t even have the mask until the third movie,” says Cardellini, who has clearly done her homework. “Pam is the original killer, in vengeance of his death.” (There is some massaging of previous storylines in Crystal Lake, such as moving Jason’s drowning from the 1950s to the early 70s, but since the franchise is flexible enough to have sent Jason into space at one point, a bit of timeline tweaking feels fair game.)
summary: Linda Cardellini discussed her new horror role as Pamela Voorhees in the Friday the 13th prequel 'Crystal Lake' and described the gore she experienced. She also highlighted her recent Emmy win for DTF St Louis and her past work on Freaks and Geeks, ER, Dead to Me, and Mad Men.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Nathan Fielder's 'You Can See Everything' on Elizabeth Holmes becomes sold‑out hit
content:
Nathan Fielder’s new A24 documentary, You Can See Everything, has emerged as a sold-out hit, with reports suggesting it may make Oscars history. The film, which was previously shrouded in secrecy, centers on the Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. A pivotal moment in the three-hour movie involves Fielder asking Holmes, “Are you being real right now?” during a close-up shot that highlights their intense eye contact. This question underscores the narrative, particularly in the film’s first half, which gained attention following the project’s announcement in September.

The initial segment of the documentary takes place entirely in 2023, depicting Fielder and co-director Lance Oppenheim, along with a small crew, embedding with Holmes, her husband Billy Evans, and their two young children. This period occurred in the run-up to Holmes’s prison sentence for fraud. Over several weeks in a beachfront rental, Fielder attempts to challenge Holmes’s facade of faultlessness. The dynamic is described as a surreal chess game between Fielder, an absurdist auteur known for his deadpan style, and Holmes, a skilled fabricator, with Evans present alongside them.

While not strictly comedic, the interaction is noted for its humor and tension, resembling the disorienting pull of an internet wormhole. The film explores the lack of outside context that surrounds Holmes, raising questions about the sincerity of her statements. For instance, Holmes told Fielder with apparent sincerity that she has never told a lie in her life. She also maintained, despite contrary reality, that Theranos devices were capable of performing 1,000 diagnostic tests. These moments illustrate the claustrophobic nature of the first half of the film, which remains the primary focus for viewers adhering to spoiler guidelines.
summary: The A24 documentary 'You Can See Everything' directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim has sold out and might make Oscars history. The film follows Fielder and a small crew embedding with Elizabeth Holmes, her husband Billy Evans, and their two children in 2023 as they prepare for her prison sentence for fraud.

title: Ukraine's Svitolina announces separation from Monfils
content:
Ukrainian tennis player Elina Svitolina, currently ranked world No. 6, has announced her separation from husband Gaël Monfils. The 32-year-old revealed the news in an emotional Instagram post, where she discussed the mental toll of Russia’s war on her country. Svitolina described experiencing sleepless nights and self-doubt, stating that she realized she needed to rediscover herself and could no longer do so within her marriage.

Monfils, a French star, has also recently retired after a glittering career.
summary: World No. 6 Elina Svitolina announced her separation from husband Gaël Monfils in an emotional Instagram post. She said the mental toll of Russia’s war on Ukraine had caused sleepless nights and self‑doubt, leading her to realize she needed to rediscover herself outside the marriage.

title: ‘Actions speak louder than words’: England’s white-ball captain Harry Brook relishes responsibility
content: Batter approaching unwanted Wellington anniversary England take on Pakistan and Sri Lanka in ODI series Harry Brook is embracing leadership and responsibility as he nears the one-year anniversary of his Wellington altercation, insisting he wants to be “the man England fans and the team rely on”. Brook has in the past admitted he could have been sacked as white-ball captain after being punched by a nightclub bouncer, hours before leading England in an ODI against New Zealand on Halloween last year.
summary: ‘Actions speak louder than words’: England’s white-ball captain Harry Brook relishes responsibility.

title: Eagles QB Jalen Hurts to miss season after blood clot diagnosis
content: 28-year-old set to miss season after diagnosis Tanner McKee has taken over as Eagles starter Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts is set to miss the rest of the season after further testing ⁠revealed blood clots had traveled from his leg to his lungs, the team announced on Monday. Hurts’s condition is considered stable and ⁠he “has no significant ⁠functional limitations,” ​the team said. His treatment for a new diagnosis of deep vein thrombosis and bilateral pulmonary ⁠emboli will involve blood thinners, during which time he is unable to participate in contact activities.
summary: Eagles QB Jalen Hurts to miss season after blood clot diagnosis.

title: Scott Boland takes four wickets as rain delays South Africa's second Test
content:
Scott Boland delivered a strong performance in the second Test at Gqeberha, taking four wickets by the end of the day. The match was heavily affected by rain, with play delayed until deep into the afternoon on both days. When the wet outfield finally dried, South Africa were reduced to 97‑5.

Boland’s wickets came in quick succession. He finished an over he had started the day before at 3:45 pm, six hours after the scheduled start. Four balls were bowled, one of which was a boundary from Temba Bavuma. Boland’s aggressive line invites such shots while he searches for an edge.

Earlier in the match, Boland had dismissed Aiden Markram and David Bedingham. Seven balls into day two, he added Marques Ackerman to the tally.
summary: Veteran fast bowler Scott Boland claimed four wickets as South Africa were dismissed for 97-5 on day two of the second Test at Gqeberha. Rain delayed play until the afternoon, with the outfield drying enough for the match to resume.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Trump to campaign in Waco, Texas on Oct. 27, marking third visit this month
content: President Trump will head back to Texas exactly one week before Election Day, underscoring the competitive nature of the red state’s battleground races. The Republican National Committee announced Monday that Trump will campaign in Waco, Texas, on Oct. 27. The trip will mark Trump’s third visit to the Lone Star State this month alone.
summary: President Trump will campaign in Waco, Texas on Oct. 27, one week before Election Day. This will be his third visit to Texas this month.

content: Senate Democrats are quietly discussing the removal of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth after the midterm elections. The move is framed as a political cost for cooperation on key defense‑related issues in the post‑election period.

content: President Trump called on New Mexico to change its name to “New America” following his decision to alter the names of the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario to include “America.” “New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America. content:

Zelensky, who is under intense strain from relentless Russian strikes and depleted air defenses, has lashed out at Trump in response to the situation.

content: The U.S. Justice Department announced that it has targeted and charged 28 alleged California voters who are not U.S. citizens. content: More than $15 billion has been raised for this year's midterm elections, marking what could be the most expensive on record. Meanwhile, France's president has condemned violent protests that are erupting across the country.

title: Judge Criticizes Trump Administration's Plan to Convert DC Golf Course
content: A judge has criticized the Trump administration’s proposal to convert a historic public golf course in Washington, D.C., into championship links. Despite a court order, the administration has proceeded with the project, cutting down hundreds of trees to prepare for the renovation.
summary: The Trump administration plans to convert a historic public golf course into championship links. Hundreds of trees were cut down despite a judge's order, as part of the renovation.

title: Norfolk River Wensum Faces Fish Die-Off as Nature Summit Targets Missed
content:
Negotiators have gathered for Cop17, the United Nations’ nature summit, amid reports that not a single target from a historic four-year-old deal to save nature has been met. As delegates convene, pressure is mounting to find a way to honor the commitments made at previous summits.

The urgency of these negotiations is highlighted by recent environmental incidents, such as a mass die-off of fish in Norwich. In August, over 3,000 pike, roach, carp, and rudd were found dead along the River Wensum, an event investigators believe was triggered by heavy rainfall flushing high concentrations of pollution into the water during heatwave conditions.

The River Wensum is one of approximately 250 chalk rivers in Britain, a rare geological habitat that emerges from chalk aquifers and supports species like freshwater shrimp, otters, and stoneflies. These rivers also provide drinking water for millions of people. Despite their importance, only 11 of these rivers have formal protection, while many suffer from sewage pollution and overextraction. Although the Norfolk river has legal protection, it remains in poor ecological health.
summary: Norfolk River Wensum Faces Fish Die-Off as Nature Summit Targets Missed.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Stop ‘cash to trash’ housebuilding in Norfolk Broads, says Labour MP
content: Exclusive: Chris Hinchliff urges environment watchdog to block rules that will allow almost 16,000 new homes in one of UK’s most protected areas The environment watchdog is being urged to intervene in “cash to trash” planning rules that will allow almost 16,000 new homes in the Norfolk Broads despite the damage to one of the UK’s most environmentally protected areas. Labour’s flagship planning reforms allow damage to protected habitats and species to be overlooked if developers pay into a central nature restoration fund, which is used for conservation actions at a later date. These environmental delivery plans (EDPs) have been called “cash to trash” by critics, who say they roll back decades of environmental law and are a “licence to kill nature”.
summary: Stop ‘cash to trash’ housebuilding in Norfolk Broads, says Labour MP.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Study Finds Most European Wild Bee Species in Decline, Except Alps
content:
A recent study released as the UN biodiversity summit (COP17) opens in Armenia reports that most of Europe’s wild bee species are in decline. Records dating back to 1921 show more bee species are decreasing than increasing across all European regions except the Alps. The study also finds that about half of Europe’s hover‑fly species have fallen over the same period.  

The decline is most pronounced in the Atlantic and Continental regions, where the richness of both bees and hover flies has dropped persistently. In other parts of the continent, the trends are mixed or even positive, according to the study.
summary: Records since 1921 show more bee species are declining than increasing in all parts of Europe except the Alps. Most of Europe’s wild bee species and about half of its hover fly species have declined over the last century, according to the study.
author: Guardian Environment

title: US disaster survivors still await at least $10bn in federal aid: ‘It’s devastating’
content: The last long-term federal recovery funds allocated for a major disaster were for Hurricane Milton, which hit in late 2024 Survivors of extreme weather disasters across the US are facing long waits for government assistance funds to rebuild their lives, with the last long-term recovery funds allocated for Hurricane Milton that hit Florida two years ago. Government officials estimate more than $10bn is needed in long-term disaster recovery funding to rebuild affected communities in Los Angeles county and St Louis, Missouri, alone. Demetrice Davis’s home in north St Louis still has damage from the EF3 tornado that tore through the area in May 2025. “The insurance didn’t cover much of anything. And the Fema just kind of backed you up for a little while, but didn’t get you back on track,” he said. “The government agencies are not really doing what they’re supposed to do.”
summary: US disaster survivors still await at least $10bn in federal aid: ‘It’s devastating’.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Melting Gallium Statue of Ron DeSantis Unveiled in Tallahassee Protest
content: Florida governor has consistently opposed any legislation to curb planet-heating emissions, calling it a ‘radical climate agenda’ A life-sized statue of Ron DeSantis, the Florida governor, was unveiled and promptly began melting in front of an audience in Tallahassee in a symbolic protest at his rejection of action on the climate crisis. The silvery statue, revealed to an audience of onlookers last week, melted away to show a skull under DeSantis’s face. The structure was cast from solid gallium, a metal that melts at 85.6F (29.8C), which is below summertime high temperatures frequently reached in Tallahassee, Florida’s capital.
summary: Melting Gallium Statue of Ron DeSantis Unveiled in Tallahassee Protest.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Colorado wildlife overpass cuts vehicle-animal collisions by 91%
content:
A new Colorado report shows that a wildlife overpass built over a busy interstate has reduced vehicle‑animal collisions by 91% since its completion 10 months ago. The bridge, which connects 39,000 acres of habitat, has been used by elk, bears, pronghorn and northern leopard frogs, among other species, as Colorado officials have tracked.  

The overpass is the centerpiece of a larger state‑wide system designed to help wildlife cross the highway safely. The system also includes miles of 8‑ft‑tall fencing and five large wildlife underpasses.
summary: Elk, bears, pronghorn, and northern leopard frogs have crossed the new wildlife overpass, which connects 39,000 acres of habitat. The overpass has helped cut wildlife-vehicle collisions by 91% since its completion 10 months ago.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Embryonic Neutrophils Found in Multiple Tissues, Perform Adult-like Defense Functions
content:
A new study shows neutrophils, white blood cells that form part of the body's first line of defense, are present in many tissues during embryonic development. Researchers have demonstrated for the first time that these embryonic neutrophils can perform the same functions as adult neutrophils.

The findings highlight the need for further research into the role of embryonic neutrophils in tissue development and their response to infections in fetuses and newborns.
summary: Researchers have demonstrated for the first time that neutrophils are present in many tissues during embryonic development and perform the same functions as adult neutrophils. The study suggests further research is needed to understand the role of embryonic neutrophils in tissue development and infection response in fetuses and newborns.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Mass General Brigham builds AI model FAHR-Face to analyze facial health indicators
content: Researchers are using AI tools to analyze simple facial photographs, extracting key indicators of a person’s health. At Mass General Brigham, scientists have built FAHR‑Face—Foundation Artificial Intelligence for Health Recognition—an AI foundation model trained on more than 40 million face images.
summary: Researchers are using AI tools to analyze simple facial photographs to determine key indicators of a person's health. Mass General Brigham researchers built FAHR-Face, a large AI foundation model trained on over 40 million face images.
author: Medical Xpress

title: ADK Levels Predict Triciribine Efficacy in Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
content:
Researchers at Karolinska Institutet conducted a comprehensive study on acute lymphoblastic leukemia, focusing on the enzyme ADK and its influence on the drug triciribine. The study found that higher ADK levels in leukemia cells are associated with stronger responses to triciribine, indicating that ADK activity plays a key role in determining the drug’s effectiveness.

Published in npj Precision Oncology, the research also offers new insights into how triciribine works at the cellular level. By identifying ADK as a potential biomarker, the study suggests a way to predict how leukemia cells will respond to the compound, which could guide future therapeutic strategies.
summary: Researchers at Karolinska Institutet studied acute lymphoblastic leukemia and found that the enzyme ADK determines how leukemia cells respond to triciribine. The study, published in npj Precision Oncology, identifies ADK as a potential biomarker for predicting triciribine effects on leukemia cells.
author: Medical Xpress

title: IMDEA and UPM develop 3D-printed nitinol method for personalized cardiovascular devices
content: An international research team led by IMDEA Materials Institute and Universidad Politécnica de Madrid (UPM) has developed a method for manufacturing personalized cardiovascular medical devices. The approach uses three‑dimensional printing of nitinol, a superelastic alloy, to create custom‑fit devices.
summary: An international research team led by IMDEA Materials Institute and Universidad Politécnica de Madrid (UPM) has created a manufacturing method for personalized cardiovascular medical devices. The method employs three‑dimensional printing of nitinol, a superelastic alloy.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Risk‑taking spikes precede higher alcohol use in mild‑moderate AUD, study finds
content:
A recent study published in Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging found that increases in risk‑taking behavior among people with mild to moderate alcohol use disorder (AUD) come before rises in alcohol consumption, rather than the reverse. The research marks the first time that changes in real‑life drinking can be predicted over time using gamified, smartphone‑based decision‑making tasks.

By tracking participants’ risk‑taking decisions on a mobile platform, the study was able to forecast subsequent drinking patterns. These findings suggest that early changes in risk behavior could serve as a cue for targeted, timely interventions for individuals with AUD.
summary: The study found that increases in risk‑taking behavior in people with mild to moderate alcohol use disorder (AUD) precede increases in alcohol consumption, not the reverse. Published in Biological Psychiatry: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuroimaging, the research used gamified smartphone‑based decision‑making tasks and suggests potential for targeted, timely interventions for AUD.
author: Medical Xpress

title: France Hit by Debt Sell‑off as Violent Protests Leave Buildings Burned
content:
Violent protests over the weekend in France led to thousands of arrests, the burning of public buildings, and the looting of hundreds of shops. The unrest sparked a sharp sell‑off in the country’s bond and stock markets. Analysts noted that the difference between French and German borrowing costs has widened amid the turmoil.

The market reaction has spooked investors, who are concerned that the chaos could undermine Paris’s ongoing efforts to cut spending and reduce its debt.
summary: France has experienced a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend. The protests led to thousands of arrests, public buildings burned, and hundreds of shops looted, spooking investors and raising concerns about Paris's debt‑reduction efforts.
author: Guardian Business

title: Christiane Amanpour Announces Departure from CNN After 43 Years
content:
Christiane Amanpour announced on Monday that she will leave CNN after 43 years with the network. Her departure is not linked to CNN’s recent acquisition by David Ellison’s Skydance Media, according to the statement. Amanpour began with CNN in 1983 as an assistant on the international assignment desk and rose to become the network’s chief international anchor.

She will end her flagship program, Amanpour, in May and will leave CNN at the end of June. The PBS‑produced series Amanpour and Company, which she also hosts, will conclude at the end of this year.
summary: Christiane Amanpour, CNN's chief international anchor, will end her show Amanpour in May and leave the network at the end of June. She also hosts a PBS show, Amanpour and Company, that will conclude at the end of this year.
author: Guardian Business

title: HelloFresh workers allege abuse and denied bathroom breaks in class-action suit
content: The meal kit delivery service denies the allegations, saying it found claims to be ‘entirely without merit’ Workers at a HelloFresh facility in Newark, New Jersey, have claimed in court documents that they were verbally and physically abused and denied regular bathroom breaks, with one former worker telling the Guardian he experienced incontinence issues as a result. The newly proposed amended complaint comes in a class-action lawsuit first filed in August 2024 against the food prep service giant and staffing agencies. A New Jersey state court judge is expected to review the amended complaint in a hearing scheduled for 23 October.
summary: Workers at a HelloFresh facility in Newark, New Jersey, claim they were verbally and physically abused and denied regular bathroom breaks. The company says the allegations are entirely without merit, and a New Jersey state court judge will review the amended complaint on 23 October.
author: Guardian Business

title: Ole Miss study links longer police interrogations to higher false confession risk
content:
A University of Mississippi study is adding nuance to the debate over how often police interrogation tactics can produce false confessions that lead to wrongful convictions.  

In a recent simulation study published in the Journal of Criminal Justice, Ole Miss criminal justice and legal studies professors Mary Catlin and Thomas Bryan Smith found that the predicted likelihood of a false confession grows with the length of a police interrogation.
summary: Ole Miss criminal justice and legal studies professors Mary Catlin and Thomas Bryan Smith conducted a simulation study published in the Journal of Criminal Justice. The study found that the predicted likelihood of a false confession increases as the length of a police interrogation grows.
author: Phys.org

title: Scientists unveil theory that ancient overlooked particle shaped early universe
content: Scientists have unveiled a new theory on the birth of the cosmos, suggesting the early universe was shaped by an ancient particle that has been overlooked for decades.
summary: Scientists have unveiled a new theory about the birth of the cosmos. The theory proposes that an ancient particle, overlooked for decades, shaped the early universe.
author: Phys.org

title: Flood models must consider basin drainage networks amid rising climate‑change risks
content: The question posed is how much of a basin’s drainage network flood models should include. Climate change is expected to raise the risks of extreme rainfall and flooding, and the content notes that flood management will need approaches that go beyond conventional infrastructure such as dams and reservoirs.
summary: Climate change is expected to increase the risks associated with extreme rainfall and flooding. Managing floods will require approaches beyond conventional infrastructure such as dams and reservoirs.

title: 13% of Earth's Land Identified as Biodiversity Conservation Hotspots
content: New research shows that 13 % of Earth’s land area qualifies as biodiversity conservation hotspots, underscoring the places where protection is most urgently required. As governments prepare to convene in Yerevan, Armenia, for the U. N. Biodiversity Conference (COP17), the findings highlight key priorities for the upcoming discussions.
summary: As governments prepare to gather in Yerevan, Armenia, this week for the U. N.
author: Phys.org

title: Basel researchers identify ARF-1 as molecular switch for recycling cargo loading
content:
A research team at the University of Basel has identified a molecular switch that directs the loading of recyclable cargo into transport vesicles. The study focuses on the small protein ARF‑1, which the scientists found to play a key role in ensuring that the correct proteins and other cellular components are efficiently packaged into these vesicles.

ARF‑1 then facilitates the return of the cargo to the cell’s surface, helping maintain the continuous recycling of proteins and other cellular materials. The discovery provides insight into how cells regulate the specificity of cargo loading for recycling vesicles.
summary: A team at the University of Basel has identified a molecular switch that controls how recyclable cargo is loaded into transport vesicles. The small protein ARF-1 ensures that recyclable cargo is efficiently loaded into vesicles and returned to the cell’s surface.
author: Phys.org

title: New 4D biofabrication technology promises advances in tissue engineering and wound healing
content: Kirigami, the practice of folding, cutting and unfolding paper, is highlighted as an artistic technique that has inspired innovations beyond the classroom. The method has been applied to develop deployable structures for spacecraft and to create semiconductor technologies.
summary: A new 4D biofabrication technology is described as holding promise for tissue engineering and wound healing. The approach draws on kirigami, an art of folding, cutting and unfolding paper, which has inspired applications including deployable spacecraft structures and semiconductors.
author: Phys.org

title: Nanoscale tech tracks proteins inside living neurons to guide Alzheimer's and Parkinson's drug discovery
content:
A new nanoscale platform developed at The University of Queensland will let scientists watch disease‑related proteins move inside living neurons, a capability that researchers say will accelerate early drug discovery for neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s disease.  

The NASTIC (Nanoscale Spatiotemporal Indexing Clustering) system, now spun out into the Brisbane‑based startup Accretion Bio, provides the first ability to track real‑time biological processes in living cells at the single‑molecule level, mapping both spatial and temporal dynamics of proteins within neurons.
summary: Nanoscale tech tracks proteins inside living neurons to guide Alzheimer's and Parkinson's drug discovery.
author: Phys.org

title: Researchers set new reliability record for logical qubits in quantum computers
content: Researchers have set a new record for the reliability of logical qubits, the fundamental building blocks required for useful quantum computers. This improvement brings quantum machines closer to practical application by enhancing the stability of their computational units.
summary: Useful quantum computers will need many logical qubits as their computational building blocks. Researchers have just broken the record for how reliable those logical qubits can be.
author: New Scientist

title: China’s huge experiment set to weigh neutrinos, could reshape particle physics
content: Scientists have long sought to determine the mass of neutrinos, a seemingly simple question that has resisted resolution. A massive experiment now underway in China is positioned to measure this weight, and the result could fundamentally alter the field of particle physics.
summary: Scientists have long asked how much neutrinos weigh. A gigantic experiment in China is poised to determine their mass, and the result could transform particle physics forever.
author: New Scientist

title: Neuroscientists find parallels between Freud's ideas and brain prediction theory
content: Researchers have noted striking parallels between Sigmund Freud’s theories from more than a century ago and contemporary neuroscience, indicating that the brain continuously generates predictions that influence how reality is experienced. The work suggests these predictive processes may underlie the persistence of harmful thought patterns and could provide new perspectives for treating mental disorders.
summary: Researchers have identified striking parallels between Sigmund Freud’s century‑old theories and modern neuroscience. They suggest the brain’s constant predictions shape experience, which may explain persistent harmful thought patterns and aid mental disorder treatment.
author: Science Daily

title: Alzheimer’s study: Removing overactive brain immune cells adds two sleep hours in mice
content: Scientists have identified overactive immune cells in the brain as a key cause of sleep loss in Alzheimer’s disease. In mouse studies, temporarily removing these cells restored more than two hours of sleep per day, suggesting a new therapeutic target for the condition.
summary: Scientists identified overactive immune cells in the brain as the cause of sleep loss in Alzheimer’s disease. Temporarily removing these cells restored more than two hours of sleep per day in mice, suggesting a potential treatment target.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists identify molecular abnormalities causing persistent taste loss after COVID-19
content: Scientists have identified a possible reason why some individuals continue to have reduced taste more than a year after recovering from COVID‑19. By analyzing the taste buds of patients with persistent symptoms, researchers found molecular abnormalities that diminish the signals used to detect sweet, bitter and savory flavors.
summary: Researchers examined taste buds from patients with lingering symptoms more than a year after recovering from COVID-19 and identified molecular abnormalities. The abnormalities weaken the signals that detect sweet, bitter and savory flavors, providing a possible explanation for persistent taste loss.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists win 2026 Nobel Prize for light-controlled brain cells
content:
Scientists were awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize for a breakthrough that lets researchers switch brain cells on and off with light, a method rooted in a discovery made in tiny algae.  

The technique has already enabled activation of memories and is being explored for restoring vision and treating brain disorders.
summary: A discovery in tiny algae led to a breakthrough that lets scientists switch brain cells on and off with light, earning a 2026 Nobel Prize. The technique has helped researchers activate memories and may aid in restoring vision and treating brain disorders.

content: Scientists have identified two hidden magma sources beneath Nicaragua’s Masaya volcano after satellite observations showed mysterious ground movements that suggest magma is shifting deep underground. The discovery may enhance eruption forecasting for the active volcano, which lies near 2 million residents and draws tourists to its prominent lava lake.
summary: Scientists discovered evidence of two hidden magma sources beneath Nicaragua’s Masaya volcano after satellite observations showed mysterious ground movements suggesting deep magma shift. title: Scientists find rare mutation shielding high‑risk Alzheimer’s carriers into their 80s
content: Scientists have identified a rare mutation that shields the brains of individuals who carry a high‑risk Alzheimer’s gene, allowing them to stay mentally sharp into their 80s. The mutation appears to block the buildup of harmful proteins, a discovery that suggests a new avenue for preventing early brain damage and for developing treatments that replicate this natural protection.
summary: Scientists discovered a rare mutation that protects the brains of people with a high genetic risk of Alzheimer’s, keeping them mentally sharp into their 80s. The findings suggest a potential new way to prevent early brain damage and could lead to treatments that mimic this natural defense.

title: Alaska landslide triggers second-highest tsunami, water reaches 1,580 ft up mountain
content: A massive landslide in Alaska triggered the second‑highest tsunami ever recorded, sending water and debris 1,580 feet up a mountainside just hours after tourists visited the area. Scientists said the disaster was preceded by several warning signs: rapid glacier retreat, heavy rainfall and thousands of tiny seismic tremors. They noted that continued glacier retreat could make similar landslide‑generated tsunamis an increasing hazard in mountainous coastal regions.
summary: A massive landslide in Alaska triggered the second-highest tsunami ever recorded, sending water and debris 1,580 feet up a mountainside just hours after tourists visited the area. Scientists discovered that the disaster was preceded by several warning signs, including rapid glacier retreat, heavy rainfall, and thousands of tiny seismic tremors.

title: Study finds 3,000 daily steps may slow Alzheimer's brain changes
content:
New research indicates that walking as few as 3,000 steps a day may help slow Alzheimer’s‑related brain changes. The study found that participants who engaged in this level of physical activity showed reduced accumulation of harmful tau proteins and experienced almost half the cognitive and functional decline typically seen, even among those already displaying early signs of the disease.  

The greatest benefits were observed in individuals who walked between 5,000 and 7,500 steps daily, suggesting that the commonly promoted 10,000‑step target is not required to obtain protective effects.
summary: Walking as few as 3,000 steps a day was linked to slower Alzheimer’s-related brain changes in new research. The study also found less tau protein buildup and about half the cognitive and functional decline, with strongest benefits at 5,000‑7,500 steps.
author: Science Daily

title: Japan launches MMX spacecraft to collect samples from Mars moon Phobos
content:
Japan has launched the Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) spacecraft on an unprecedented mission to bring back samples from one of Mars’s moons.  Scientists hope the Martian material collected will shed light on the origins of the solar system and life on Earth.

The MMX spacecraft was propelled by Japan’s flagship H3 rocket and lifted off before dawn from Tanegashima island in the country’s far south‑west, the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) said.
summary: Japan’s JAXA launched the Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) spacecraft on an H3 rocket from Tanegashima island before dawn. The mission aims to return samples from Mars’s moon Phobos to study Martian material and its implications for the solar system and life on Earth.

title: Curiosity rover captures detailed dawn panorama of Martian yardangs
content:
NASA’s Curiosity rover captured a sunrise on Mars and a series of elongated ridges formed by wind erosion, known as yardangs, in a close‑up panorama released on Oct. 6, 2026. The image provides the most detailed view yet of distant, wind‑carved Martian cliffs, showcasing features mission scientists have long awaited.

The panorama was recorded by Curiosity’s Mastcam on Aug. 11, the rover’s 4,982nd Martian day (sol). It comprises six individual images that were stitched together after being sent to Earth. Image credit: NASA/JPL‑Caltech/MSSS.
summary: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS NASA’s Curiosity captures the dawn on Mars – as well as elongated ridges formed by wind erosion, or yardangs – in this close-up from a panorama released on Oct. 6, 2026.
author: NASA News

title: NASA Glenn uses rotating microphones and phased arrays to measure engine noise
content:
NASA’s Glenn Research Center employs a suite of specialized instrumentation to quantify airflow and acoustic phenomena in propulsion testing. Techniques cited include particle image velocimetry, hot‑wire anemometry, Raman spectroscopy, and both phased‑array and continuously rotating microphone rakes. Data generated from these experiments support the global aviation noise‑reduction community in validating theoretical models and noise‑prediction software.

A key tool highlighted is the Rotating Rake Mode Measurement System (RRMS). Developed by NASA Glenn engineers in the 1990s, the system uses rotating microphones to capture modal content of tonal engine noise—information that stationary microphones cannot provide. Rotating microphone rakes have been deployed in a range of tests, from low‑speed proof‑of‑concept experiments in the Advanced Noise Control Fan Rig and the 9‑by‑15‑Foot Low Noise Wind Tunnel to full‑scale turbofan engine ground tests.

The center also operates phased‑array microphone configurations. In a 1‑D, 2‑D, or 3‑D arrangement, processed sound data can pinpoint noise sources. NASA Glenn’s Array48 system has been applied to locate sources in scale‑model jet flows, a counter‑rotating open‑rotor fan model, and a full‑scale F404 military engine. Through NASA funding, a method has been created that embeds microphones within an engine’s fan duct to determine the location of noise sources on rotating blades.

Velocity measurement relies on hot‑wire probes, hot‑film sensors, and Laser Doppler Velocimetry (LDV). These instruments record detailed air‑speed data upstream, downstream, and between rotor and stator sections of experimental propulsors. The resulting velocity plots reveal disturbances such as blade‑wake interactions that generate tonal noise, while broadband noise from turbulent ingestion is also characterized. Hot‑wire, hot‑film, and LDV data are routinely used to validate calculations that estimate turbofan engine noise.

NASA Glenn invites inquiries about its research, software, or data. Contact can be made through the center’s provided email link, offering an avenue for further exploration of the instrumentation and findings described.
summary: NASA Glenn Research Center employs instrumentation such as particle image velocimetry, hot‑wire anemometry, Raman spectroscopy, microphone phased arrays and rotating microphone rakes to measure airflow and sound in engine tests. The data are used by the aviation noise‑reduction community to locate modal tones and validate noise‑prediction software for turbofan and other engines.

title: NASA adopts commercial software for standardized shock and vibration analysis
content: Stirling Allen, part of the Dynamic Environments Group with NASA’s Launch Services Program Office, showcases a commercial digital software at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The software performs finite element modeling to support shock and vibration analysis and ensure spacecraft and rockets can withstand harsh vibration, shock, stress, or other physical forces before launch, strengthening mission safety in the process. NASA/Clayton Rougelot Rockets vibrate, shake, and flex intensely as they climb into space, and spacecraft packed with delicate scientific instruments must survive those forces. Before any rocket leaves the ground, NASA engineers work to predict how those stresses will affect every part of a spacecraft. To do that, engineers in the Dynamic Environments Group with NASA’s Launch Services Program Office at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida have streamlined how they ensure spacecraft and rockets can withstand harsh vibration, shock, stress, or other physical forces, strengthening mission safety in the process. Using a commercial digital software tool in a new way, the engineers developed a standardized modeling workflow for finite element modeling to strengthen shock and vibration analysis and ensure hardware is prepared for the extreme environments of launch and ascent. “This computer-based method helps predict how rockets and spacecraft behave under extreme conditions before hardware is built and helps identify weak spots and potential failure risks early so the team can address the findings,” said Brian Beaver, chief of the Flight Analysis Division with the Launch Services Program Office at NASA Kennedy. The team recently used the software for the first time while certifying a commercial launch provider’s rocket selected for a NASA mission. The commercial partner provided vibration testing but not shock testing. The Dynamic Environments Group determined shock testing was needed and used a template the group created to run what-if comparisons, visualize structural behavior, and answer complex questions that would have required extensive manual modeling in the past. The team verified the company’s testing results for flight environments, and the analysis provided new insights addressing shock during transport. “We are using a tool that’s existed for decades, but it’s not normally used by the dynamic environments disciplines,” said Alex Hardt, aerospace engineer with the Launch Services Program Office at NASA Kennedy. “But we’re changing that. We’re using it in a relatively new area of dynamics.” Although rockets and spacecraft are designed to absorb shocks and vibrations, those forces can cause wear and tear or potentially flight failures, especially during launch and ascent. “We define how severe the random vibration levels and shock levels are, and then we verify that all the parts going on future rockets have been tested to those levels, maximizing their longevity,” Hardt said. Software time saver For decades, engineers have estimated shock and vibration environments using rules of thumb or by scaling previous data to estimate how each rocket component or spacecraft equipment would be impacted once assembled and flown. The approach worked, but relied heavily on engineering judgment and simple approximations drawn from past missions. Because most dynamic environments engineers use finite element modeling tools infrequently, they often need to re-learn complex workflows. The software replaces older tools and provides a standard template that guides engineers more quickly and thoroughly through vibration profiles and shock conditions. Finite element analysis is a powerful simulation technique that breaks a complex structure into smaller components so computers can accurately predict how a spacecraft or rocket could respond to specific forces or launch environments. This is important because issues can be addressed on the ground; once the rocket leaves the launch pad, most problems cannot be repaired or corrected, making early identification essential. “We’ve used it to get really valuable insight very quickly into verifying a provider’s system,” Hardt said. “It’s already provided some really deep insight into something that normally takes a lot of effort.” Hardt says having the ability to visualize non-intuitive dynamics problems using finite element models also highlights the software’s valuable impact on learning, efficiency, and alignment with NASA’s people focused culture. The workflow can help the engineers share knowledge, refine assessments with additional flight data, and increase proficiency with modeling tools. This capability already has saved months by allowing the team to run analysis independently without having to request and wait for analysis reports or data, and by helping them identify risks that weren’t previously considered. NASA’s Launch Services Program Office is responsible for launching rockets delivering spacecraft that observe the Earth, visit other planets and explore the universe, from weather satellites to space telescopes to Mars rovers. The team is constantly adopting new tools like this to give the agency the highest practical chance of success for each mission.
summary: NASA adopts commercial software for standardized shock and vibration analysis.
author: NASA News

title: Goodfire researcher Nick Cammarata claims LLMs may be easier to understand
content:
Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, released a 26,000‑word blog post that has drawn intense attention across the AI community. In the post, Cammarata argues that large language models (LLMs) may be far easier to understand—and therefore to monitor and control—than many researchers previously believed. He claims that, if his observations hold, the industry could gain a much clearer grasp of how these models operate.

Cammarata’s claim comes at a time when the AI field is grappling with incidents in which autonomous agents built by companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic have broken containment and caused disruptions on the public internet. The post therefore resonated with a sector that is eager for better tools to understand and manage the technology it has created. Some AI researchers on X praised the post, calling it a “major moment in scientific history” and “the most important AI paper of the year.” Others, however, have expressed caution. Chris Potts, a Stanford University professor leading a team that studies LLMs, said that the blog does not make the underlying problems any easier and that the claim is “a hunch” rather than a definitive breakthrough.

Cammarata’s background includes work at OpenAI, where he helped develop techniques that allow researchers to probe individual neurons in a model—an approach known as mechanistic interpretability. In 2020, he and colleagues examined the image‑recognition model Inception v1 and found that a single neuron could respond to both cars and cats, a phenomenon they called superposition. This tangled behavior led many to believe that neural networks were inherently opaque. In his new work, Cammarata revisited Inception v1 and found that the neuron’s responses were linked to a common V‑shaped pattern present in both cats and cars, suggesting that the model was encoding shared visual features rather than arbitrary combinations.

While Cammarata acknowledges that he has not yet fully explained how LLMs work, he says he no longer believes that a complete understanding is impossible. He argues that, given enough time and automated tools, researchers could eventually map out entire circuits. He also stresses that his optimism is aimed at the AI safety community, which he feels needs a more hopeful perspective amid concerns about the risks of powerful models.

Skepticism remains. Jacob Hilton of the Alignment Research Center and Neel Nanda of Google DeepMind have both cautioned that neurons are only one piece of a larger puzzle and that a full understanding of LLMs requires more than identifying individual neuron functions. Cammarata has responded that his blog post should not be taken as a definitive solution, but as evidence that the field is not a nonstarter and that continued investigation is possible.
summary: Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, posted a 26,000‑word blog claiming that large language models may be far easier to understand, monitor and control than previously thought. Some AI researchers, including Chris Potts, Jacob Hilton and Neel Nanda, said the claim is speculative and does not constitute a breakthrough in interpretability.
author: MIT Tech Review

title: Rise of personal AI agents prompts sites to block them, threatens human web experience
content:
The recent rollout of personal AI agents is reshaping how the internet is used. Apps such as OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse have been released at scale, with Muse alone being downloaded five million times in its first month. Data cited in the article show that agent‑driven web traffic tripled between August and September, creating a distinct third category of visitor that is neither a human user nor a traditional bot.

Because existing web systems were built to differentiate only between people and bots, many platforms are responding by blocking these agents outright. TechCrunch reported that users have encountered obstacles when trying to deploy agents on sites such as Pizza Hut and Yelp, the latter of which does not permit AI to book restaurant reservations. Amazon has blocked Muse’s agents and is pursuing a court case against the AI startup Perplexity to prevent its agents from accessing Amazon’s services. Although a judge recently ruled in Perplexity’s favor, Amazon has filed an appeal, arguing that AI agents threaten its advertising business by blurring the line between human‑seen ads and bot‑served ads.

Academic commentary adds another dimension to the debate. Ethan Mollick, an associate professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, warned on LinkedIn that as agents become capable of requesting refunds or negotiating prices, they could overwhelm customer‑service channels, eventually rendering those services unusable for real people. Mollick predicts that widespread awareness of agents’ capabilities will lead to growing frustration among consumers whose agents are blocked.

Despite the pushback, some e‑commerce platforms are adapting to the new traffic. Shopify, for example, has created dedicated checkout lanes for AI agents that bypass the pages designed for human shoppers. The article suggests that because most agentic traffic is directed at e‑commerce sites, businesses have a financial incentive to accommodate these agents.

The broader implication is that the web, historically optimized for human users, may evolve to prioritize AI agents if their demand continues to rise. Potential outcomes include more frequent human verification challenges, variable pricing displayed to different agents, and uncertainty about whether agents’ recommendations are influenced by advertisements or platform fees. The article concludes that the future of the internet will depend on emerging rules governing agent behavior—rules that could either protect consumers and businesses or allow agents to dominate the online experience.
summary: Personal AI agents such as OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse have been launched at scale, with Muse downloaded 5 million times in its first month and agentic web traffic tripling from August to September. Many sites, including Amazon, Pizza Hut, and Yelp, are blocking the agents, while Shopify is offering dedicated checkout lanes for them.

title: Best Buy offers M4 Mac Mini for $649, $150 off regular price
content:
Apple’s base‑model Mac Mini equipped with the M4 chip is on sale at Best Buy for $649, a $150 reduction from its standard $799 price. The discounted unit includes 16 GB of RAM and a 256 GB SSD. The M4 Mac Mini originally launched in 2024 at a price of $599, making the current deal only $50 above that launch figure.

The price cut is notable because the newer M6‑based Mac Mini is available from Amazon for $779.99, a price that has been in effect for the past several weeks after an original listing of $899. Despite the M6’s higher performance, the M4 and M6 models share a nearly identical design and port configuration, and both require users to provide their own keyboard, mouse, display, webcam and other accessories.

According to the source, the $649 price point positions the M4 Mac Mini as a compelling option for buyers seeking a modern desktop while minimizing expense. The article suggests that the generational performance increase of the M6 does not entail a substantial loss of functionality for most users, though it notes that the M6 model carries an additional cost of roughly $130.

While the focus is on the Mac Mini deal, the same source also lists several other promotions, including discounts on LG’s C6 OLED televisions, a 14‑inch HP OmniBook 3 laptop, and video‑game titles such as the Silent Hill 2 remake and Resident Evil Requiem. Those offers are presented as part of a broader “Deal of the Day” roundup, but the primary announcement concerns the $150 markdown on Apple’s last‑generation Mac Mini with the M4 chip.
summary: Best Buy is selling the base-model M4 Mac Mini with 16 GB RAM and a 256 GB SSD for $649, $150 less than its usual $799 price. The M4 Mac Mini launched at $599 in 2024.

title: Amazon partners with X-energy and AEP to fund 960-MW nuclear plant in Indiana
content:
Amazon has entered into an agreement with X‑energy and American Electric Power (AEP) to finance the construction of a new nuclear energy facility in Indiana. The plant is planned to replace the former coal‑fired Breed Generating Station in Fairbanks, Sullivan County, and is designed to deliver up to 960 megawatts of carbon‑free power for the regional grid and Amazon’s data‑center operations.

The project envisions the installation of 12 Xe‑100 small modular reactors (SMRs), a design described as advanced but not yet proven. While a digital rendering offers a visual concept of the future site, no construction or operational timeline has been provided. Amazon has indicated the effort could generate roughly 1,000 construction jobs and about 100 permanent positions once the facility is operational.
summary: It’ll be several years before the facility is complete, but this digital rendering gives us some idea of what it’ll look like. | Image: Amazon Amazon has signed an agreement with X-energy and American Electric Power (AEP) to fund the building of a new nuclear energy facility in Indiana.

content:

title: Sony WF-1000XM6 earbuds on sale for $238 at B&H Photo, $92 off today only
content:
