title: Alliance Arts delays demo of Drunken Goddess Reflex over AI cloning fears
content:
The video game industry has long relied on developers creating clones of competing titles, a practice that has varied in originality and platform enforcement. Recent advances in AI coding tools have accelerated the cloning process, prompting some creators to become more cautious about sharing early work.

Developer Alliance Arts highlighted this trend over the weekend. The group postponed the launch of a planned public demo for its demon‑themed Russian Roulette drinking game, Drunken Goddess Reflex, which was originally set to debut alongside today’s Steam Next Fest. In a social‑media post on Friday evening, the Alliance Arts team explained that, besides concerns about managing streaming restrictions, they feared the demo’s content could be quickly imitated or replicated with AI or other tools. They worried that such copies might be released before their own launch.
summary: Alliance Arts delayed the public demo of its demon-themed Russian Roulette drinking game Drunken Goddess Reflex, which had been scheduled for Steam Next Fest. The team said they feared AI coding tools could quickly imitate or replicate the demo’s presentation and gameplay, allowing copies to be released before their launch.
author: Ars Technica

title: ReactOS adds NTFS installation support, removing FAT32 requirement
content:
ReactOS has announced a major milestone: the operating system can now be installed directly onto an NTFS partition. Previously, installations required a FAT32 partition, a limitation that the project has now overcome and which brings it closer to a beta release.

NTFS is a proprietary Microsoft file system that originated with Windows NT 3.1 in 1993 and has remained the standard since the variant introduced with Windows XP in 2001. ReactOS’s stated goal of achieving binary compatibility with Windows Server 2003 made the FAT32 restriction a practical barrier to reproducing a Windows‑like environment.

The new NTFS driver, while functional, still lacks caching, journaling, and security support, resulting in inferior performance. The ReactOS team cautioned that there may be undiscovered bugs and advised users to proceed with care.
summary: ReactOS can now be installed directly onto an NTFS drive partition, ending the previous requirement for a FAT32 partition. The new NTFS driver lacks caching, journaling and security support and may contain undiscovered bugs.
author: Ars Technica

title: Endurance Energy tests subsea geothermal plant at Axial Seamount, generates brief power
content:
A Seattle‑based startup, Endurance Energy, completed the world’s first subsea geothermal power plant demonstration near the Axial Seamount, an active underwater volcano located almost a mile below the ocean surface. The three‑week test, carried out in September, used a 3‑ton prototype that produced less than 10 seconds of net‑positive electricity, proving the technical feasibility of extracting renewable energy from the deep ocean.

Endurance Energy plans to commercialize subsea geothermal power for Pacific island nations and other customers who seek alternatives to costly fossil‑fuel imports. In an email to Ars, founder and CEO Andrew Redd explained that the deep ocean supplies unlimited cold seawater for cooling and that the water’s weight keeps the system and well pressurized, allowing the plants to remain compact.
summary: The world's first demonstration of a subsea geothermal power plant was carried out near the active Axial Seamount volcano about a mile below the ocean surface. A three‑week test of a 3‑ton prototype by Seattle‑based startup Endurance Energy produced less than 10 seconds of net‑positive electricity, showing the technical feasibility of subsea geothermal power.
author: Ars Technica

title: Plex media server vulnerabilities exploited to install cryptominers and proxy software
content:
A researcher has warned that recently patched vulnerabilities in Plex Media Server are being actively exploited. Plex released fixes for four vulnerabilities at the beginning of last month, and three weeks later CVE listings identified five vulnerabilities, one rated 8.6 out of 10 for severity. The researcher disclosed an exploit that links four of the flaws to achieve remote code execution on a device running a vulnerable Plex version, naming the chain “Plex2Shell.”

Using the new details, another researcher set up a honeypot that mimics a Plex server. Within a day the honeypot recorded active scanning and successful exploitation attempts. In the observed attacks, two payloads have been installed: a cryptominer that mines cryptocurrency for the attacker’s wallet, and residential‑proxy software that lets users route traffic through the compromised device, often for illicit purposes. Users are advised to apply the latest Plex patches promptly.
summary: Plex media server vulnerabilities exploited to install cryptominers and proxy software.
author: Ars Technica

title: Haiwei Zhou study: lithium‑ion battery production 0.18% of GHG, could rise tenfold by 2050
content:
A new study led by Haiwei Zhou at the University of Melbourne examined the greenhouse‑gas emissions generated in the production of lithium‑ion batteries, a key component of the energy transition that includes electrifying vehicles and heating while sourcing electricity from renewables. The researchers note that, although battery‑related emissions are currently modest—accounting for about 0.18 percent of annual global releases—they could rise by tenfold or more by 2050 as battery use expands.

The study identifies several avenues for lowering these emissions. Certain elements used in lithium‑ion chemistries require more energy to mine and refine, and the manufacturing process itself involves multiple steps that could be made more energy‑efficient. Additionally, recycling battery materials can re‑introduce them into the supply chain while consuming far less energy than primary mining.
summary: The first order of business for the energy transition is electrifying applications like vehicles and heating and making sure that the electricity that powers them is made using renewables. But once the dominant slices of the emissions pie have shrunk, other categories with less potential to reduce emissions become important.
author: Ars Technica

title: Accused OpenAI spy had folder called “Saudi Gov Docs,” FBI says
content:
A U.S. court on Monday approved the government’s request to keep a former OpenAI engineer in detention, denying his release while prosecutors build a case that he covertly recorded a top‑secret conference‑room and stole proprietary information from the company’s Frontier lab.  

U.S. Attorney Craig Missakian argued that Abdulrahman Alfozan must remain detained as the government alleges he spied on OpenAI, potentially for personal profit or to aid the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. The filing notes that Alfozan communicated with a Saudi royal family member via WhatsApp and was exploring options to relocate permanently to Saudi Arabia amid the country’s expanding AI initiatives.  

According to FBI findings cited in the filing, Alfozan accessed a folder titled “Saudi Gov Docs” on his iPhone and allegedly stored photographs of a second listening device he had placed in OpenAI offices. The case remains under investigation.
summary: Accused OpenAI spy had folder called “Saudi Gov Docs,” FBI says.
author: Ars Technica

title: Russian satellite Kosmos 2612 maneuvers in extreme proximity to US imaging satellite ICEYE‑X36
content: A Russian military satellite maneuvered in "extreme proximity" of a commercial Earth-imaging satellite in recent days in the first known example an unsanctioned rendezvous in low-Earth orbit, according to the orbital intelligence company LeoLabs. The Russian spacecraft, Kosmos 2612, "conducted a deliberate series of maneuvers toward ICEYE-X36, a US-operated commercial imaging satellite," LeoLabs said. "Kosmos 2612 closed from hundreds of kilometers away to extreme proximity to ICEYE-X36. It then maneuvered around ICEYE-X36, remained nearby for an extended period, and then began moving away." US military officials and independent analysts have tracked Kosmos 2612 since its April launch on a Soyuz rocket from a spaceport in northern Russia. Within weeks, it became apparent that at least four of the six satellites from that launch were stalking ICEYE-X36 after they adjusted orbits to line up with the orbit of the ICEYE spacecraft. Read full article Comments
summary: LeoLabs reported that the Russian military satellite Kosmos 2612 conducted a deliberate series of maneuvers that brought it to extreme proximity with the US‑operated commercial imaging satellite ICEYE‑X36. Within weeks of its April launch on a Soyuz rocket, at least four of the six satellites from that launch were observed stalking ICEYE‑X36.
author: Ars Technica

title: Pennsylvania health department issues alert as congenital measles returns after decades
content:
Pennsylvania’s health department released a health alert on Monday warning that cases of measles in pregnancy—and consequently congenital measles—are on the rise. The advisory notes that congenital measles had not been observed in the state for decades before the current outbreak, which the department says continues to spread across Pennsylvania.

The alert provides detailed clinical guidance for handling measles exposures and cases during pregnancy as well as infections in newborns. It highlights that many physicians have not encountered such cases in their careers because of the long‑term success of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.

State data as of October 19 show 1,286 measles cases reported this year in 42 counties, with 247 hospitalizations and six reported deaths, the latest of which remains under investigation before being added to the official count. The department links the surge to declining vaccination rates nationwide, which it says allow the highly infectious virus to spread in under‑vaccinated communities.
summary: Pennsylvania's health department issued a health alert Monday as cases of measles in pregnancy and, in turn, cases of congenital measles have continued to increase. Before the current outbreak—which continues to rage across the state—congenital measles cases hadn't been seen in decades, the department noted in its advisory.
author: Ars Technica

title: Replika founder Eugenia Kuyda launches AI assistant from Disrupt pitch
content: Eugenia Kuyda, the founder of Replika, has launched a new venture called Wabi. The startup brings to market a personal AI assistant—free and downloadable to anyone—that builds on an idea she originally pitched at Disrupt more than a decade ago.
summary: She built the AI assistant she originally pitched at Disrupt 12 years ago. Her new startup Wabi now offers the personal AI assistant for free as a downloadable app.
author: TechCrunch

title: Hackers breach OpenCode platform, steal API keys and raise user AI charges
content: OpenCode, an open‑source AI coding agent that has become a popular alternative to Claude Code and Cursor, suffered a security breach. Hackers accessed part of its online platform, stole some users’ API keys and triggered charges on the affected users’ AI accounts. Attempts to enlist other AI tools for assistance were declined, as those tools refused to examine the malicious code.
summary: Hackers accessed part of OpenCode’s online platform and stole some users’ API keys, which ran up charges on their AI accounts. The AI tools OpenCode turned to for help refused to examine the malicious code.
author: TechCrunch

title: Amazon launches TorchNeuron tool to challenge Nvidia's dominance in PyTorch
content: Amazon has introduced a new development tool called TorchNeuron. The company says the tool is intended to challenge Nvidia’s dominance of PyTorch, the free framework used to build most AI applications, by encouraging developers to run their models on alternative processors, including Amazon’s own chips.
summary: Amazon introduced the TorchNeuron development tool to target Nvidia's lead in the PyTorch ecosystem. The company says the tool will help developers run AI applications on alternative chips, including Amazon's own hardware.
author: TechCrunch

title: Hugging Face policy chief says embedded AI evaluators are not an easy solution
content: Hugging Face’s chief policy officer, Irene Solaiman, told TechCrunch that embedded AI evaluators are not an easy solution. She noted AI labs rely on model benchmarking—a system presented as neutral and accurate for comparing products—but the evaluation methods are complex and still maturing.
summary: AI labs have staked their reputations on model benchmarking, a supposedly neutral system to measure whether one AI product is better than another. Irene Solaiman, Hugging Face’s chief policy officer, said at a TechCrunch discussion that the methods behind these evaluations are complicated and still maturing, making embedded AI evaluators not an easy solution.
author: TechCrunch

title: ICMP warns AI trained on Kylie Minogue songs as tech firms pressure Australia
content:
The International Confederation of Music Publishers (ICMP) has warned the Australian government that it is the only country among dozens approached to relax copyright laws that is considering doing so. The ICMP, which represents major labels such as Sony, Warner and Universal along with thousands of independent publishers worldwide, said that artificial‑intelligence systems have already been trained on the works of Australian artists, including Kylie Minogue and Nick Cave, without compensation.

The body cautions that tech companies are attempting to “strong‑arm” the government into weakening copyright protections. It urges Australian officials to resist these pressures and maintain the current legal framework that protects artists’ rights.
summary: The International Confederation of Music Publishers says AI systems have already been trained on songs by Australian artists such as Kylie Minogue and Nick Cave without compensation. It warns that Australia is the only country among dozens approached that is considering weakening copyright law despite pressure from tech firms.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Australian groups call stronger workplace privacy as AI tracking of staff rises
content:
Calls are being raised in Australia to strengthen workplace privacy as employers increasingly adopt AI‑powered monitoring. The Human Technology Institute has warned that technology ranging from CCTV to keystroke tracking is being used to track workers’ movements, a trend that is accelerating with the introduction of AI.

The institute supplied examples to Guardian Australia. One fast‑food restaurant uses surveillance cameras to prevent employees from using their phones. In another case, AI tracking led to a cashier being warned for a mistake that occurred once every 533 scans.

Monitoring tools are common across factories, office jobs, delivery work and retail, and are often deployed without employees being informed of the extent of the surveillance.
summary: Australian groups call stronger workplace privacy as AI tracking of staff rises.
author: Guardian Technology

title: AI tool from Mass General Brigham predicts cancer survival from a single selfie
content: Doctors have created an artificial‑intelligence system that can estimate a person’s biological age and predict a cancer patient’s chances of survival using a single photograph of the face. The tool was custom‑built by experts at Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit, integrated academic health‑care system in Massachusetts. According to the study, the AI directly predicts survival outcomes for patients diagnosed with cancer based solely on the facial image.
summary: Doctors have developed an artificial intelligence system that can estimate biological age and predict cancer survival from a single facial photograph. The tool was custom-built by experts at Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit integrated academic healthcare system in Massachusetts.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Report finds US teens can download nudify apps despite Apple and Google controls
content:
A report by the Tech Transparency Project found that U.S. teens can reach “nudify” applications even though Apple and Google offer parental‑control features. Using test accounts presented as 13‑year‑olds, the project downloaded 135 apps that include tools for generating non‑consensual nude imagery.

The report cites a December 2025 incident in Pennsylvania: Morgan Dorfman learned that a student at her daughter’s high school was using an artificial‑intelligence image‑editing app called Movely to produce sexual videos from photographs of her daughter and five other girls. The case illustrates how such apps are being accessed by minors despite existing platform safeguards.
summary: Using test accounts posing as 13‑year‑olds, the Tech Transparency Project downloaded 135 apps that can generate non‑consensual nude imagery. In December 2025, Morgan Dorfman learned that a student at her daughter’s Pennsylvania high school used the AI app Movely to create sexual videos from images of her daughter and five other girls.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Demonstrators block Louvre entrances in Paris on Monday
content: Demonstrators blocked the entrances to the Louvre in Paris on Monday. The action took place as tensions stayed high after a weekend of protests, clashes and looting across France.
summary: Demonstrators blocked the entrances to the Louvre in Paris on Monday. The action occurred as tensions remained high after a weekend of protests, clashes and looting in France.
author: Euronews

title: Qatar prepares new regional defence partnership and warns of imminent energy peak
content: Qatar is preparing a new regional defence partnership and says it will keep diplomatic channels open with Tehran, asserting that dialogue and economic ties can foster lasting peace. Doha also warned that an energy‑disruption “peak” is imminent, with further difficulties expected in the coming days and months.
summary: Qatar is preparing a new regional defence partnership while keeping channels open with Tehran. Doha warned of an energy disruption “peak” that could bring further difficulties in the coming days and months.
author: Euronews

title: Rubio centers Trans‑Caspian trade and critical minerals at C5+1 meeting in Samarkand
content: At a C5+1 meeting in Samarkand, the United States and five Central Asian governments endorsed closer transport and industrial cooperation. U.S. Secretary of State Antony Rubio highlighted Trans‑Caspian trade and critical minerals as central topics of the talks and conducted bilateral discussions. During the same session, Uzbekistan signed the Artemis Accords.
summary: The United States and five Central Asian governments backed closer transport and industrial cooperation at a C5+1 meeting in Samarkand. Rubio held bilateral talks and Uzbekistan signed the Artemis Accords.
author: Euronews

title: French National Rally aims to exploit protests with law‑and‑order rhetoric
content: In the wake of the weekend's violence, the political camps have been trading blame for the “chaos”. The riots have played into the hands of the far-right National Rally, which has been quick to capitalise on the anger and fears over law and order. FRANCE 24's Emerald Maxwell takes a look.
summary: The weekend's violence sparked riots that prompted political camps to trade blame for the chaos. The far‑right National Rally quickly sought to capitalize on anger and fears over law and order.
author: France 24

title: France faces policing scrutiny after violent weekend protests over cost of living
content: France reeled on Monday after a weekend of nationwide unrest sparked by mass protests over the rising cost of living and in support of high‑school students’ demands for education funding. The clashes turned violent, leaving both law‑enforcement officers and protesters wounded, while public buildings were set ablaze and businesses were looted. The scale of the disorder has prompted renewed scrutiny of the French police’s approach to maintaining public order.
summary: France faces policing scrutiny after violent weekend protests over cost of living.
author: France 24

title: AI photos falsely depict elderly couple stripped during France riots
content: AI‑generated images that claim to show an elderly couple “stripped and robbed” amid unrest in France have attracted millions of views. The pictures were amplified by far‑right accounts and have been used to promote inflammatory claims about Muslims, Jews and the riots. FRANCE 24 Observers traced one of the images to an AI photo montage posted by a pro‑Israel account, confirming that the images were created with OpenAI tools. The alleged assault has not been verified, and no official reports confirm that such an attack occurred.
summary: AI-generated photos falsely claiming to show an elderly couple being “stripped and robbed” during unrest in France have racked up millions of views. The images, traced by FRANCE 24 Observers to an AI montage posted by a pro‑Israel account and created with OpenAI tools, remain unverified with no official reports confirming the alleged assault.
author: France 24

title: Le Pen seeks to boost popularity using weekend riots, expert says
content:
After violence erupted over the weekend, political camps have been trading blame for the resulting chaos.  
The riots appear to have benefited the far‑right National Rally, which has quickly capitalised on the anger and fears surrounding law and order.  
Speaking with France 24’s Mark Owen, Dr David Lees, Reader in French Studies at the University of Warwick, said Marine Le Pen is trying to use these events as a vehicle for pushing her popularity ahead of next year’s elections.
summary: The weekend's violence sparked blame between political camps and benefited the far‑right National Rally. Dr David Lees said Marine Le Pen is trying to use the events to push her popularity ahead of next year's elections.
author: France 24

title: France orders Vinted, eBay and Amazon to curb resale of looted items
content: France’s government has asked major second‑hand marketplaces—including Vinted, eBay and Amazon—to crack down on listings that appear to involve stolen goods after weekend violence and looting left thousands of shop owners reeling. The request targets suspicious adverts that have surfaced online.
summary: Thousands of shop owners are reeling from weekend violence and looting, and listings of apparently stolen items have appeared online. France's government asked major second‑hand marketplaces Vinted, eBay and Amazon to crack down on suspicious adverts.
author: France 24

title: Four dead as torrential rain floods eastern Spain, Valencia sees 700 L/m²
content: Torrential rain battered eastern Spain on Monday, causing floodwaters to sweep away cars, submerge roads and strand residents. The flooding killed at least four people in recent days. Emergency crews in Valencia carried out more than 400 rescues, where rainfall reached 700 litres per square metre in 24 hours in some areas.
summary: Torrential rain battered eastern Spain on Monday, killing at least four people as floodwaters swept away cars, submerged roads and stranded residents. Emergency crews carried out more than 400 rescues in Valencia, where rainfall reached 700 litres per square metre in 24 hours in some areas.
author: France 24

title: Korean writer You Yeong-Gwang's debut novel The Rainfall Market a massive success
content: You Yeong‑Gwang’s debut novel, The Rainfall Market, tells the story of a mysterious hidden shop that only opens when it rains. The book achieved massive success despite the author’s unknown status.
summary: You Yeong-Gwang's The Rainfall Market tells the story of a mysterious hidden shop that only opens when it rains. The debut novel by an unknown author was a massive success.
author: DW World

title: Thailand allows Myanmar refugees legal work, first year shows gaps
content: A year after Thailand authorized long‑staying refugees from Myanmar to work legally, the policy has been welcomed by refugees and rights groups. However, those groups note that the program’s first year has revealed significant shortcomings.
summary: A year ago Thailand granted long‑staying refugees from Myanmar the right to work legally. Refugees and rights groups welcomed the move but said the program’s first year exposed significant shortcomings.
author: DW World

title: Rubio visits India, skips New Delhi to tour world's largest oil refinery
content: Washington’s top diplomat, Rubio, will visit India this week, bypassing New Delhi to tour the world’s largest oil refinery. The refinery processes massive amounts of Russian crude. The trip has prompted speculation about whether Trump is seeking a new deal.
summary: Washington's top diplomat Rubio will visit India this week, skipping New Delhi and instead touring the world's largest oil refinery that processes massive amounts of Russian crude. Is Trump looking for a new deal?
author: DW World

title: Ethiopia installs new Tigray administration as Eritrea tensions spark war fears
content:
Ethiopia has installed a new administration in the conflict‑hit region of Tigray after federal forces pushed back Tigrayan fighters.  

Despite this development, tensions with Eritrea persist, raising fears that the conflict could expand into a wider regional war.
summary: Ethiopia has installed a new administration in conflict-hit Tigray after federal forces pushed back Tigrayan fighters. Tensions with Eritrea continue to raise fears of a wider regional war.
author: DW World

title: Canada: Alberta votes on holding independence referendum
content: Alberta is holding a vote on whether to hold an independence referendum. Analysts say the province is not likely to approve a genuine breakaway plebiscite, but the separatist movement hopes the vote will give it leverage over Mark Carney’s government.
summary: Canada's oil-rich western province of Alberta is not deemed likely to vote in favor of a real breakaway plebiscite. Nevertheless the separatist movement hopes to gain leverage over Mark Carney's government.
author: DW World

title: Bulgaria Issues Arrest Warrants for German Nationals Over Starlink Antenna Fires
content: A Bulgarian court has issued arrest warrants for two young German nationals suspected of setting fire to Starlink antennas and is seeking their detention in Germany. The incident is noted as reminiscent of a similar case in Poland, which Warsaw attributes to Russian orchestration.
summary: A Bulgarian court has issued arrest warrants for two young German nationals suspected of setting fire to Starlink antennas. The case is reminiscent of another in Poland, which Warsaw says was orchestrated by Russia.
author: DW World

title: At least four killed as torrential rain floods eastern Mediterranean coast of Spain
content: At least four people died in Spain after torrential rain battered the country’s eastern Mediterranean coast. The severe flooding left more than 450 people stranded on rooftops, in buildings or in cars.
summary: At least four people have died in Spain as torrential rain battered the eastern Mediterranean coast. The severe flooding left more than 450 people stranded on rooftops, in buildings or in cars.
author: DW World

title: UN biodiversity chief urges urgent action at Yerevan conference
content: At the UN Biodiversity Conference in Yerevan, Armenia, the top UN official emphasized that biodiversity losses continue to upend the lives of billions of people. He said future prosperity depends on countries taking urgent action to protect the planet, placing the protection of Earth’s fragile biodiversity in the spotlight.
summary: Biodiversity losses continue to upend the lives of billions of people. The top UN official leading talks at the UN Biodiversity Conference in Yerevan said on Monday that countries need to take urgent action to protect the planet.
author: UN News

title: World Food Programme cuts Gaza food aid, affecting 500,000 as winter nears
content: The United Nations World Food Programme announced on Monday that funding shortages have compelled it to cut food assistance in the Gaza Strip by roughly one‑third. The reduction will leave about 500,000 people without aid as winter approaches.
summary: Funding shortages have forced the World Food Programme to slash assistance to hungry families in the Gaza Strip by roughly one third. The cut will affect about 500,000 people as winter approaches, the UN agency announced on Monday.
author: UN News

title: Guterres honors four Indonesian peacekeepers killed in Lebanon
content: UN Secretary-General António Guterres paid tribute to Indonesian peacekeepers on Monday, laying a wreath in honour of four who recently lost their lives in Lebanon and offering a robust defence of UN peacekeeping in what he called “testing times for peace”.
summary: Guterres honors four Indonesian peacekeepers killed in Lebanon.
author: UN News

title: Israeli attacks kill six in Gaza and UN urges protection for West Bank olive farmers
content: Israeli attacks on Gaza over the weekend killed at least six Palestinians, including children, despite a year‑old ceasefire agreement. In the occupied West Bank, settler violence persisted during the olive harvest, prompting UN independent experts on Monday to call on Israel to protect Palestinian farmers.
summary: Israeli attacks on war‑torn Gaza over the weekend killed at least six Palestinians, including children, despite a year‑old ceasefire agreement. UN independent experts on Monday urged Israel to protect Palestinian farmers as settler violence continued during the West Bank olive harvest.
author: UN News

content:
Elections in Haiti remain on hold as gangs adjust to a security crackdown.  

The United Nations told the Security Council on Monday that armed groups are adapting to intensified security operations, stepping up reprisals against civilians and extending their reach into rural areas.
summary: Elections in Haiti are on hold as gangs adjust to the intensified security crackdown. The UN warned the Security Council on Monday that armed groups are increasing reprisals against civilians and extending their reach into rural areas.

content: UN human rights chief Volker Türk said on Monday that more than a quarter of humanity struggles to obtain enough food even though global production is sufficient for everyone. He described hunger as “an avoidable tragedy” and attributed it to injustice and the denial of human rights.
summary: More than a quarter of humanity struggles to get enough food even though the world produces enough for everyone, UN human rights chief Volker Türk said on Monday. He blamed injustice and the denial of human rights for hunger in a world of plenty.
author: UN News

title: Car U-turn hits MP Helen Haines twice in alleged targeted attack
content:
A car allegedly performed a U‑turn before striking Independent MP Helen Haines twice, an incident that some witnesses believe may have been a targeted attack near her electorate office. Police are interviewing the alleged attacker in Wangaratta, Victoria, where the incident occurred.  

Haines was air‑lifted from Wangaratta to Melbourne’s Alfred Hospital for emergency surgery on Monday night. She remains in critical but stable condition following the attack.
summary: A man accused of making a U-turn rammed independent MP Helen Haines's vehicle twice near her electorate office, according to eyewitnesses. Haines was airlifted from Wangaratta to Melbourne's Alfred Hospital, where she remains in critical but stable condition after emergency surgery.

title: Barber Ricky Jefferies hailed as hero by PM after intervening in Helen Haines attack
content:
Barber Ricky Jefferies said he had just finished cutting hair when he intervened after a driver allegedly struck independent MP Helen Haines in what police describe as a deliberate attack. According to Jefferies, he grabbed and held the driver at the scene, saying he had “no choice” but to step in.

The Australian prime minister later praised Jefferies as a hero for rushing out of his shop to help Haines. Jefferies was standing outside his barbershop on Tuesday morning; the shop is located next to Haines’ electorate office in Wangaratta. He described himself as “almost shy” about the attention the incident generated.
summary: Ricky Jefferies said he had just finished cutting hair when he grabbed and held the driver who allegedly deliberately struck independent MP Helen Haines. The Australian prime minister hailed Jefferies as a hero for rushing out of his shop to help Haines.

title: Hurricane Trudy weakens to tropical storm after Mexico warnings; one dead in Greece floods
content:
Hurricane Trudy, the 22nd named system of the Pacific season, weakened to a tropical storm after prompting coastal warnings for southwestern Mexico. While the category‑2 hurricane was positioned roughly 100 miles (160 km) southwest of the Mexican coast, the U.S. National Hurricane Center issued hurricane warnings for the coastal portions of Jalisco, Michoacán and Colima, forecasting sustained winds of 60‑90 mph on Sunday. Expected rainfall totals of 100‑150 mm raised concerns about flooding, landslides, a dangerous storm surge and damaging waves along the onshore‑wind zones of the region. By Monday morning Trudy had downgraded to a tropical storm and the coastal warnings were lifted.

In Greece, heavy rains caused deadly floods that resulted in one confirmed fatality. No further details were provided about the extent of the flooding or additional impacts.
summary: Hurricane Trudy, a category 2 system about 100 mi southwest of Mexico’s Pacific coast, prompted hurricane warnings for Jalisco, Michoacán and Colima with winds of 60‑90 mph and heavy rain. By Monday the storm had weakened to a tropical storm and warnings were lifted, while flooding in Greece killed one person.

title: Eighth Ebola case in Kenya highlights US quarantine center controversy
content: Opposition to US-led quarantine center in Kenya follows sweeping funding cuts and withdrawal from WHO An eighth person in Kenya has tested positive for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola in the country’s first-ever cluster of cases of the virus, as the second-largest outbreak in history has killed more than 4,300 and sickened more than 9,000 people in the region. It highlights the diminished role the US has played in the worsening Ebola outbreak by building a controversial quarantine center in Kenya, pulling back health support globally, and banning travelers from certain countries. All of this has also reduced the ability to identify and respond to the outbreak and exacerbated mistrust.
summary: Eighth Ebola case in Kenya highlights US quarantine center controversy.

content: A drone strike hit a market area in the town of al‑Dibab, West Kordofan state, in southern Sudan on Sunday evening, killing 80 people, most of whom were commuters catching rides home. The attack struck twice at a transport hub near the market, making it one of the deadliest single attacks of the war. Witness Ahmed Wadi said he helped bury 50 bodies, including his brother Mohamed, after the strike.
summary: A drone strike near a market in al-Dibab, West Kordofan, southern Sudan on Sunday evening killed 80 people, mostly commuters catching rides home. Witness Ahmed Wadi said he helped bury 50 bodies, including his brother Mohamed.

content:
A Kenyan court has found Paul Mackenzie and approximately 30 others guilty of murder for the deaths of 190 children and one adult. Prosecutors stated that Mackenzie and his church established a sect that ordered followers to starve themselves and their children. The verdict marks one of the world’s worst cult-related disasters in recent history.

summary: A Kenyan court found Paul Mackenzie and about 30 others guilty of murder for the deaths of 190 children and one adult. Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after a tipoff, and authorities later uncovered bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest in south‑eastern Kenya.

title: US grants temporary deportation reprieve to over 100,000 Ukrainian and Sudanese migrants
content: DHS says migrants ‘retain protections’ after temporary protected status was set to expire on Monday Send us your questions about immigration and the midterms More than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan can stay in the United States without immediate risk of deportation, the Department of Homeland Security said, in what amounts to a temporary reprieve after their right to stay in the country was set to expire on Monday. title: Japan Launches MMX Sample-Return Mission to Mars Moon Phobos Today
content:
Japan is set to launch a bold sample‑return mission to Mars’ moon Phobos today, October 19. The Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft will lift off from Japan’s Tanegashima Space Center on an H3 rocket at 3:41 p.m. Eastern Daylight Time (1941 GMT), which is 4:41 a.m. local Japan time on October 20. Viewers can watch the launch live through Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) coverage that begins at 2:45 p.m. EDT (1845 GMT).

MMX’s primary objective is to study Mars’ two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, and to return samples from Phobos to Earth. Phobos is about 14 miles (22 km) wide, while Deimos measures roughly 8 miles (13 km). Their origins remain uncertain; they may be remnants of a massive impact on Mars or captured asteroids, according to Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters. NASA partners on the mission by providing a scientific instrument, a technology demonstration, communication support, and funding for American scientists on the MMX team.

The spacecraft is scheduled to arrive in the Mars system in August 2027, then enter orbit around Phobos a month later. It will conduct a 18‑month study of both moons before deploying the French‑German Idefix rover onto Phobos’ surface in early 2029. Idefix, weighing 55 pounds (25 kg) in Earth gravity, will perform two main tasks: gathering information to prepare for the main spacecraft’s sample‑collection landing and analyzing the composition and texture of Phobos’ surface. On the moon’s low gravity, Idefix will weigh only about 15 grams (0.5 ounces). The MMX mothership will land on Phobos in 2030, collect at least 10 grams (0.4 ounces) of samples, and then return to Earth. The return capsule is expected to land in 2031, where scientists worldwide will examine the samples for insights into Mars and the broader solar system.

MMX was originally slated to launch in 2024, but problems with the H3 rocket delayed it. Because Mars and Earth align for interplanetary launches only once every 26 months, the mission had to wait for its next opportunity. Japan’s successful sample‑return history—including the Hayabusa mission that returned material from the asteroid Itokawa in 2010 and Hayabusa2’s return from Ryugu a decade later—underscores the country’s expertise in this field.
summary: Japan will launch the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission on Oct. 19 from Tanegashima Space Center aboard an H3 rocket. MMX will travel to Mars, orbit Phobos and Deimos, deploy the Idefix rover in 2029, collect at least 10 grams of Phobos samples in 2030, and return them to Earth in 2031.

title: Rays lead ALCS 3-2 after Drew Rasmussen's seven-inning win over Guardians
content: The Tampa Bay Rays defeated the Cleveland Guardians 3‑1, moving ahead 3‑2 in the best‑of‑seven American League Championship Series. Starting pitcher Drew Rasmussen worked seven innings, limiting the Guardians’ offense and earning praise for his performance in Game 5. Rays outfielder Jonny DeLuca noted that the presence of Rasmussen on the mound promised a quiet day for the outfielders, a prediction that held true as the pitcher subdued Cleveland’s attack on Sunday. The win puts Tampa Bay on the brink of a World Series appearance.
summary: The Tampa Bay Rays defeated the Cleveland Guardians 3-1 in Game 5 of the AL Championship Series. Drew Rasmussen pitched seven innings, quieting the Guardians' offense and giving Tampa Bay a 3-2 series lead.
author: Guardian Sport

title: South Africa host Australia at St George's Park; rain delays second Test day two
content:
The second men’s cricket Test between South Africa and Australia, hosted by the Proteas at St George’s Park in Gqeberha, experienced a delay to the start of play on day two due to rain. The weather conditions prevented the match from proceeding as scheduled, leading to a pause in the game.

Local weather radar indicated that the rain was unlikely to clear quickly, with static cloud formations observed over the town and a larger system to the east. This persistent weather prompted a period of uncertainty regarding the pitch conditions.

During the delay, the ground covers were briefly removed, leading to discussions between the umpires about a potential pitch inspection. However, the covers were subsequently replaced, ending the brief window for play. The situation highlighted the common challenges faced by cricket matches when weather conditions are unfavorable.
summary: South Africa are hosting Australia at St George’s Park for the second Test, day two. The start of play in Gqeberha was delayed by rain, and the covers were removed and replaced after an inspection.

title: Greenpeace urges COP17 leaders to treat biodiversity as public duty, not profit
content:
An Lambrechts, a biodiversity politics expert at Greenpeace International and head of the Greenpeace delegation at the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) COP17 in Yerevan, Armenia, argues that protecting nature is a public duty rather than a private profit opportunity. With COP17 marking the halfway point to the 2030 deadline set by the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the first Global Review indicates that countries are not on track to meet biodiversity targets. Lambrechts notes that while funding is insufficient, the core issue is a public policy distortion where the global economy spends approximately $30 destroying nature for every $1 invested in its protection.

The disparity is highlighted by data from the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services, which reports $2.4 trillion in public subsidies for fossil fuels, agriculture, and water use, compared to only $220 billion in global investment for biodiversity conservation and restoration. Lambrechts criticizes the current discourse, which suggests that mobilizing private capital, scaling offsets, and “derisking” investments can close the finance gap. She contends that this approach misunderstands ecological stewardship, as biodiversity is a non-monetisable public good essential for human survival, and relying on profit-seeking capital perpetuates the structural drivers of ecosystem destruction.

Instead of seeking private solutions, Lambrechts advocates for recovering public wealth lost to cross-border tax abuse, financial secrecy, and corporate impunity. She urges finance and environment ministers in Yerevan to support swift action on global tax rule reforms, the elimination of harmful subsidies, and the cancellation of unsustainable sovereign debts. In advanced economies, public funding often undermines biodiversity; for instance, Europe funnels over €5.3 billion annually into intensive forest biomass harvesting under renewable energy directives, which degrades primary forest ecosystems.

For developing countries, the reliance on private finance is complicated by a severe sovereign debt crisis. In 2024, public debt in these economies reached record levels, with net interest payments absorbing $921 billion. A record 61 developing countries now spend more than 10% of government revenue on foreign debt service, and many climate-vulnerable nations spend twice as much servicing external debt as they receive in combined climate and biodiversity finance. This financial burden forces governments into austerity measures and the expansion of raw commodity exports into pristine biomes to secure foreign exchange.

Lambrechts points to the United Nations Framework Convention on International Tax Cooperation (UNFCITC) negotiations as a potential path forward, noting that an estimated $492 billion in tax revenue is lost annually to offshore tax havens. Multinational corporations account for approximately $348 billion of this loss by shifting profits away from countries experiencing environmental degradation, with developing nations losing tens of billions annually in the mining sector alone. Additionally, illicit financial flows from illegal logging drain between $51 billion and $152 billion yearly. She concludes that leaders at COP17 must prioritize securing predictable, sufficient, and sovereign public finance for biodiversity conservation to ensure a restorative future.
summary: An Lambrechts is a biodiversity politics expert at Greenpeace International with extensive experience in biodiversity-related multilateral negotiations. She is the head of the Greenpeace delegation at the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) COP17 happening in Yerevan, Armenia.

title: Landsat 9 Captures Autumn Colors in Poland's Bieszczady Mountains
content:
On October 8, 2026, the Operational Land Imager (OLI) aboard the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 satellite captured an image of southeast Poland’s Bieszczady National Park. The imagery reveals the seasonal transformation of the Carpathian Mountains, where beech and other deciduous trees are displaying reds and golds. As air temperatures drop and daylight wanes, these trees curtail the production of chlorophyl, causing green pigments to fade and allowing yellows and reds to become visible. In the same region, brown bears are prowling the mountains with the goal of fattening up ahead of winter hibernation.

European beech (Fagus sylvatica) dominates the area’s forests, though other species such as sycamore maple (Acer pseudoplatanus) also contribute to the vibrant fall colors. The text describes the European beech as a descendant of ice-age survivors that has persisted across millennia in various climates. After glaciers retreated, beech forests spread northward across Europe from isolated refugia in the Carpathians, Alps, and other mountain ranges, playing a crucial role in reforesting previously ice-covered land. Portions of Bieszczady National Park are included within UNESCO’s network of ancient and primeval beech forests, which spans 18 countries.

In this specific area, beech forests reach elevations of approximately 1,000 to 1,260 meters (3,300 to 4,100 feet). Above this elevation lies the polonina, a Slavic term for subalpine meadow characterized by open grasslands and shrubby thickets of rowan, willows, and green alder. Patches of polonina stretching across ridge tops to the east-southeast of Smerek appear tan in the image, having lost their summer greenness.

The Bieszczady Mountains are also noted for their wildlife. European bison, which were once extinct in the wild, were reintroduced to the area in the 1960s and now roam the hills by the hundreds, according to recent surveys. The forests also provide refuge and ample food sources for populations of brown bears and Eurasian lynx. The image was created by Michala Garrison using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey, with the story written by Lindsey Doermann.
summary: The OLI instrument on the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 satellite captured images of red and gold beech forests in Bieszczady National Park on October 8, 2026. The article notes that brown bears are fattening up for hibernation while European bison, reintroduced in the 1960s, roam the area.

title: Treble Clef: Unusual X‑ray Hot Radio Source
content:
The Astronomy Picture of the Day (APOD) for October 19, 2026, features a composite image of an unusual radio source known as Treble Clef, or VLSS J0318.9+5755. This structure extends over two million light-years and resembles a common musical symbol, though its visible light is obscured by the Milky Way Galaxy. The image displays radio emission in red and recently discovered X-rays in blue.

First examined in 2004, the nature of Treble Clef remained unknown until recent observations by the Chandra X-ray Observatory and eROSITA. These findings have led to the hypothesis that the central cloud of charged particles was originally expelled by a supermassive black hole at the center of a galaxy. After the initial radio emission from these particles faded, they may have been reinvigorated by a shock wave resulting from the collision of two galaxy clusters.

The featured image is a composite of data from multiple sources. X-ray data is credited to NASA / CXC / INAF-IRA / A. Botteon et al., infrared data to UKIDSS – GPS, and radio data to ASTRON LOFAR. Image processing was handled by NASA / CXC / SAO / N. Wolk. The APOD entry notes that unusual objects like Treble Clef provide unexpected clues regarding how whole clusters of galaxies interact and the general evolution of the universe. The image is authored and edited by Robert Nemiroff, Jerry Bonnell, Cecilia Chirenti, and Keighley Rockcliffe.
summary: Treble Clef is a 2‑million‑light‑year radio structure that resembles a musical symbol and is hidden by the Milky Way. Recent Chandra X‑ray Observatory and eROSITA observations suggest its central charged‑particle cloud was expelled by a supermassive black hole and later re‑energized by a shock wave from the collision of two clusters of galaxies.

title: MIT researchers let Claude-based AI Eko explore virtual desert island for 30 hours
content:
Researchers conducted an experiment in which they stranded multiple copies of the Claude Opus 4.7 language model—nicknamed Eko—on a virtual desert island for 30 hours. The island, loosely modeled after the video game Roblox, was left unstructured, allowing the agents to write instructions that moved their avatars around the simulated environment. During this time the agents explored the limits of the world and set their own goals, such as scaling the highest point on the map or testing how high they could throw a block.

One Eko discovered that it could create new blocks by throwing and dropping a larger rock. It then began arranging these blocks on the ground to form simple patterns—hearts and pyramids—before progressing to more complex creations. The agent logged that it had “built the night sky in stone” and later drew its own name and mapped constellations such as Cassiopeia. Another iteration of Eko invented its own games, including a version of basketball and an activity resembling “the floor is lava,” in which it had to jump between small blocks without touching the ground.

The study suggests a third approach to training AI—playful learning—beyond the usual supervised or reinforcement learning paradigms. Antonio Norelli, a computer science postdoc at MIT’s Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory and a lead author on the paper, notes that the agents exhibited four hallmarks of play identified by psychologist Gordon Burghardt: inventing rules and challenges, repeating activities with slight variations, pretending objects were other objects, and pursuing goals for the sake of enjoyment. An example cited was an Eko that juggled 50 consecutive catches, then canceled the record and restarted with stricter rules.

The agents logged their activities in text files that served as long‑term memory. When later tested on specific tasks—such as moving as many objects as possible onto the island’s highest peak—the agents that had spent 30 hours playing performed better than fresh copies. Removing lines from their memory files degraded performance. While some researchers, including Nathan Cloos, acknowledge that the behavior could be role‑playing, they argue that the play contributed to learning. Critics like Eunice Yiu point out that more evidence of cognition and motivation would be needed to definitively label the behavior as play. The paper concludes that while the question of whether the agents are truly playing may not matter, the findings highlight the potential value of playful exploration for developing adaptable AI systems.
summary: MIT CSAIL researchers placed copies of the Claude Opus 4.7 model, nicknamed Eko, on a simulated desert island for a 30‑hour experiment without explicit instructions. During the run the agents built and arranged blocks, invented games and drew patterns, and later outperformed fresh copies on task tests, indicating that playful exploration can improve learning.

title: Researchers launch North Fire initiative to curb Arctic wildfires and permafrost thaw
content:
The Alaska Fire Science Consortium (AFSC) has turned a 2021 wildfire on the university’s northern campus into an educational trail to study how fires affect permafrost. In July 2021 a black‑spruce and paper birch stand ignited, possibly by lightning, and by the time fire agencies arrived the flames were 12 feet long with a 500‑foot smoke column. In 2024 the AFSC added interpretive signs to the trail. While walking the burn scar, coordinator Hilary Shook used a thaw probe to measure permafrost depth. The probe reached a concrete‑like layer about a foot below the surface, but when the fire had removed the moss and organic topsoil, the probe plunged at least three times deeper, indicating immediate thawing.

The probe’s results illustrate a broader pattern: as Arctic temperatures rise, more frequent and intense fires are accelerating permafrost thaw. The frozen soil underpins 15 % of the Northern Hemisphere’s land and stores twice as much carbon as the atmosphere. When the permafrost thaws, organic matter decomposes and releases greenhouse gases, creating a feedback loop that fuels further warming and fires. In Canada, megafires released more carbon in 2023 than the nation’s fossil‑fuel emissions combined.

To address this, Woodwell Climate Research Center, the University of Victoria’s Polis Institute for Ecological Governance, and the Alaska Venture Fund launched a multimillion‑dollar North Fire initiative. The program studies preventive measures such as controlled burns and rapid detection and suppression. A pilot in the Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge tested whether firefighters could extinguish fires threatening yedoma permafrost within 72 hours. The pilot was supported by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management’s Alaska Fire Service after the refuge manager explored the idea with Woodwell scientists.

Parallel efforts focus on early detection. The FireSat satellite constellation, managed by the Earth Fire Alliance, will provide near‑real‑time fire data worldwide. Prototype satellites launched in 2025 captured images of Alaskan wildfires, and additional operational satellites are planned for the early 2030s. The system will detect fires as small as five by five meters, potentially allowing firefighting crews to respond before fires grow large.

The North Fire initiative also explores technology‑based suppression. Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company, is testing autonomous Black Hawk helicopters equipped with thermal sensors and water tanks, while Rain Industries has software to guide unpiloted aircraft in firefighting missions. Cost estimates from a 2022 Science Advances paper suggest that intensified suppression could be cost‑effective, at roughly $12.63 per metric ton of avoided carbon dioxide, though the actual cost would depend on permafrost carbon released. The research continues to evaluate how best to allocate limited firefighting resources to protect the planet’s frozen carbon stores.
summary: Researchers launch North Fire initiative to curb Arctic wildfires and permafrost thaw.

title: Journalist deletes Instagram, embraces private life after a year
content: I’d become obsessed with appealing to my invisible audience. But since I ditched the app a year ago, my quieter moments have taken on brilliant new meaning I first downloaded Instagram when I was 17 and became hooked on it the way most people fall in love: slowly, and then all at once. For a long time, I never considered myself a social media addict. I self-righteously refused to download TikTok, declared Snapchat to be for “children”, and posted less regularly on Instagram than half of the people I followed. As I went through my university years, however, certain changes crept up on me. I began to swap reading – or essay-writing – for hours spent curating new posts. On my way home from lectures (or later, from my work as a journalist), I would spend ages trying to take the artsiest, most perfect picture of that evening’s sunset for my story – as if the people who followed me were eagerly awaiting yet another photo of one of the Earth’s rotations. What usually followed was a night of reloading my feed to see how many people had reacted to my post – or worse, hadn’t reacted at all.
summary: The author stopped using Instagram a year ago and says the change has allowed quieter, more private moments. Previously they spent hours curating posts and checking reactions, often replacing reading and essay‑writing.

title: UAE leads Gulf in disaster preparedness perception, Lebanon and Iraq fall behind
content: A recent study finds that 87 % of residents in the United Arab Emirates say their government is well prepared for disasters, while only 14 % of Lebanese citizens share that view. More than half of respondents in both Iraq and Lebanon say their governments do not care about them at all.
summary: A study found that 87% of UAE residents say their government is well prepared for disasters, compared with only 14% of Lebanese citizens. More than half of respondents in Iraq and Lebanon say their governments do not care about them at all.
author: Euronews

title: Lula and Bolsonaro trade insults in TV debate before weekend runoff
content: Lula and Bolsonaro traded insults in a televised debate ahead of the weekend presidential runoff. Experts say that, although corruption is a top concern for many Brazilian voters before the runoff, its greatest impact may be to deter people from voting rather than to change which candidate they support.
summary: Lula and Bolsonaro traded insults during a televised debate held ahead of Brazil's weekend presidential runoff. Experts say that while corruption is a top concern for many voters, it may affect whether they vote rather than which candidate they choose.
author: Euronews

title: Australia reveals three secret payloads for Ghost Shark submarine drone
content:
Australia announced that its Ghost Shark autonomous submarine drone will carry three newly disclosed payloads. The drone’s secret weapons include sea mines, logistical caches and Altius aerial drones.

The Altius drones are described as capable of both surveillance and strike missions, complementing the mine‑laying and supply‑drop functions of the other payloads.
summary: Australia has unveiled three previously secret payloads for its Ghost Shark autonomous submarine drone. The payloads are sea mines, logistical caches and Altius aerial drones capable of surveillance and strikes.
author: Euronews

title: Midday October 19, 2026 Europe news bulletin roundup
content: A midday news bulletin for October 19 2026 provides a roundup of the most important stories from Europe and beyond. The bulletin covers the latest and breaking news across categories including world, business, entertainment, politics, culture and travel.
summary: The bulletin provides a roundup of the most important stories from Europe and beyond on October 19, 2026. It covers latest and breaking news across world, business, entertainment, politics, culture and travel.
author: Euronews

title: Russia says massive strike hit Kyiv as Rubio urges Zelensky to focus on ending war
content: Russia said it carried out a “massive strike” on targets in Kyiv and the surrounding region on Monday. In the same statement, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that Washington had paused intelligence sharing with Ukraine and urged President Volodymyr Zelensky to focus on ending the war.
summary: Russia said on Monday it carried out a massive strike on targets in Kyiv and its region. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied a pause in intelligence sharing with Ukraine and urged President Volodymyr Zelensky to focus on ending the war.
author: France 24

title: Afghan economic crisis leaves EU deportees with minimal resources to return home
content: Europe's increasingly pragmatic engagement with Afghanistan's Taliban rulers is exposing a fundamental contradiction between diplomatic non-recognition and political necessity. In an investigation for The New York Times, Pakistan and Afghanistan bureau chief Elian Peltier reveals how European governments are quietly expanding negotiations with the Taliban over migrant deportations, diplomatic representation and economic assistance. “Even though on paper European governments do not recognise the Taliban administration, in practice they meet much more frequently than most of us know,” Peltier explains.
summary: Afghan economic crisis leaves EU deportees with minimal resources to return home.
author: France 24

title: French student protests expose education neglect, Axel Berra-Vescio condemns police
content:
Eve Irvine introduced Axel Berra‑Vescio, a French History‑Geography and European section teacher from the Paris region, to discuss the ongoing student protests in France. Educators involved in the demonstrations say the protests reveal years of structural neglect, widening educational inequalities and the cumulative impact of controversial reforms.

Berra‑Vescio said, “We’ve been ignored basically about every demand we made,” and condemned the police response, warning that repression is unlikely to weaken a movement rooted in long‑standing frustration over the future of public education.
summary: Eve Irvine welcomed Axel Berra-Vescio, a French History-Geography and European section teacher in the Paris region, as France’s student protests highlighted what educators describe as years of structural neglect and widening educational inequalities. Berra-Vescio condemned the police response, saying repression would not weaken a movement rooted in frustration over public education.
author: France 24

title: World Food Programme to cut aid, leaving 500,000 in Gaza without food
content: The UN World Food Programme says funding shortfalls will cut its monthly food assistance in the Gaza Strip from 1.6 million to 1.1 million people, leaving roughly 500,000 individuals without critical aid. The agency notes that two‑thirds of Gaza’s population remains acutely food insecure.
summary: World Food Programme to cut aid, leaving 500,000 in Gaza without food.
author: France 24

title: French shops demolished after weekend riots across the country
content: Protests across France sparked looting and violence, leaving shopfronts demolished and thousands of euros’ worth of stock stolen. On Sunday, President Macron held an emergency meeting with senior government officials and warned that those who looted will have to pay for the damage.
summary: Protests across France sparked widespread looting and violence, leaving shopfronts demolished and thousands of euros worth of stock stolen. President Macron held an emergency meeting on Sunday with senior government officials and warned that those who looted will have to pay for the damage.
author: France 24

title: Tirana protests enter sixth day as PM Edi Rama refuses to resign
content: Protests in Tirana continued on Sunday, marking the sixth consecutive day of demonstrations. Prime Minister Edi Rama publicly rejected calls for his resignation, the protesters’ primary demand. Since Tuesday, thousands have taken to the streets, citing poor university conditions, high tuition fees and corruption as reasons for demanding his step‑down.
summary: Protests in Tirana continued on Sunday, marking the sixth consecutive day of demonstrations. Prime Minister Edi Rama said he will not resign, while thousands of protesters demand his departure over poor university conditions, high tuition fees and corruption.
author: France 24

title: French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez says police lost control, resignation rejected
content:
France’s interior minister, Laurent Nunez, said on Monday that police “lost control” in several cities during the violent protests that broke out across the country over the weekend. He attributed the failures to a “lack of anticipation” in the authorities’ preparations.

Nunez told President Emmanuel Macron that he had submitted his resignation, saying he felt responsible for everything that happened. Macron, however, did not accept the resignation.
summary: Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police lost control in some cities during violent weekend protests. He tendered his resignation to President Emmanuel Macron, who declined to accept it.
author: France 24

title: Countries meet in Armenia to address Earth's sixth mass extinction and its impact on people
content: Human activity is accelerating plant and animal extinctions at an unprecedented pace, prompting concerns about a sixth mass‑extinction event. While nations convene in Armenia to discuss strategies for reversing nature loss, DW reports that the resulting decline in biodiversity is already causing harm to people.
summary: Human activity is driving plants and animals to extinction at an unprecedented rate. At a meeting in Armenia, countries are discussing ways to reverse nature loss, and DW reports that declining biodiversity is already harming people.
author: DW World

title: Queensland officer said Kerrie Struhs no immediate risk weeks before daughter's manslaughter
content:
A Brisbane inquest heard that Kerrie Struhs, the mother of eight‑year‑old Elizabeth Struhs, was assessed by a Queensland correctional services officer as posing “no immediate risk to others” only three weeks before the incident that led to her daughter’s death. The officer conducting the assessment did not have access to Struhs’ offending history, which includes a prior conviction for child neglect.

Struhs had previously been sentenced to five months’ jail after she failed to take Elizabeth to hospital for treatment of her type 1 diabetes in 2019. During the inquest, Coroner Ainslie Kirkegaard noted that when Elizabeth finally presented at the hospital she was “nearly dead” and in a coma. The hearing linked the recent risk assessment to the circumstances surrounding the manslaughter of the child.
summary: Kerrie Struhs was assessed by a Queensland correctional services officer as posing no immediate risk to others three weeks before the manslaughter of her eight‑year‑old daughter, Elizabeth Struhs.
author: Guardian World

title: Independent MP Helen Haines in critical condition after ‘attack’ outside Wangaratta office, PM says
content:
Independent MP Helen Haines was critically injured in an alleged attack that involved a vehicle outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, Victoria. The incident occurred on Monday afternoon, and a driver was arrested at the scene.  

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said his thoughts remain with Haines and confirmed that a man is now in custody following the alleged attack.  

The case is under investigation by the Australian Federal Police, ASIO, and the joint counter‑terror taskforce.
summary: Independent MP Helen Haines in critical condition after ‘attack’ outside Wangaratta office, PM says.
author: Guardian World

title: Pregnant women face workplace hostility and ‘sham redundancies’, Australian human rights report finds
content:
A new report from the Australian Human Rights Commission says pregnant women are being forced out of employment through “sham redundancies”, loss of shifts and hostile work environments after having a baby. The commission warns that parental discrimination continues to be a major barrier to gender equality.

The report notes that pregnancy discrimination is especially pronounced for vulnerable groups, including immigrant and First Nations women, people with disability and LGBTQ+ people. In compiling the findings, the commission held roundtables with dozens of parents, legal and community advocates.

The commission’s sex discrimination commissioner said it is “too often ‘it’s the woman who has the burden of bringing a complaint’” in parental discrimination cases. The findings highlight ongoing challenges for pregnant workers across Australian workplaces.
summary: Pregnant women face workplace hostility and ‘sham redundancies’, Australian human rights report finds.
author: Guardian World

title: Victorian premier “deeply appalled” as MP Helen Haines injured in vehicle incident in Wangaratta
content: Independent MP injured in an incident involving a vehicle outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, in regional Victoria. title: Amelia Earhart team finds no plane on Nikumaroro, debris identified as driftwood
content:
A U.S. expedition traveled to the remote Pacific atoll of Nikumaroro after researchers reported spotting a metallic glint in the waters off the uninhabited island. The team, hoping to resolve the long‑standing mystery surrounding pioneering pilot Amelia Earhart, investigated the object they believed might be her aircraft.

The investigators later determined that the suspected plane was actually a clump of washed‑up trees. “Unfortunately, we weren’t able to find that smoking gun,” said Steve Schultz of Purdue University while standing on the sand in front of a blue lagoon on Nikumaroro, an island located roughly halfway between Australia and Hawaii.
summary: Amelia Earhart team finds no plane on Nikumaroro, debris identified as driftwood.
author: Guardian World

title: Three festival float crush deaths spark safety concerns in Japan
content:
Three deaths from float crushes have heightened safety concerns surrounding Japan’s traditional festivals. The latest fatality involved Akihiro Nabae, the 62‑year‑old deputy mayor of Saijo in western Japan, who was carrying a giant float with other participants on Saturday when he became trapped beneath the structure. He was taken to hospital and later pronounced dead, while local media reported no other injuries.

The incident follows two men who died in similar float‑crushing accidents in another part of the country only days earlier, prompting renewed scrutiny of festival safety measures.
summary: Deputy mayor of Saijo, Akihiro Nabae, 62, died after being trapped under a festival float on Saturday. The death came days after two men died in similar float crush incidents in another part of Japan, raising safety concerns about traditional festivals.
author: Guardian World

title: China Q3 GDP rises 4.5% YoY, outpacing forecasts as exports surge
content:
China’s economy expanded at a 4.5 % year‑on‑year rate in the July‑September quarter, according to the National Bureau of Statistics. The growth rate surpassed economists’ expectations and was higher than the 4.3 % rise recorded in the second quarter.  

The stronger performance was driven by robust exports and a faster rise in factory output compared with consumer spending. Electronics demand helped lift industrial production, contributing to the overall GDP growth.
summary: China Q3 GDP rises 4.5% YoY, outpacing forecasts as exports surge.
author: Guardian World

title: Alberta votes Monday on staying in Canada or a second binding independence referendum
content: Voters to be asked whether province should remain part of Canada or hold a second, binding independence vote Albertans are going to the polls to decide their place in Canada, in a referendum that has exposed deep divisions within the province, not least in the separatist movement itself. On Monday, voters will respond to the question of whether Alberta should remain in Canada, or hold a second, binding independence referendum.
summary: Alberta voters will decide on Monday whether the province should remain in Canada or hold a second, binding independence referendum. The vote has highlighted deep divisions within the province, including within the separatist movement.
author: Guardian World

title: Researchers say possible Amelia Earhart wreckage may be trees on remote Pacific island
content: Researchers traveled to a remote Pacific island to investigate an object first identified in satellite imagery in 2020, assessing whether it could resolve the mystery of Amelia Earhart’s disappearance. After examination, the team concluded that the possible wreckage of Earhart’s plane is likely to be trees rather than aircraft debris.
summary: Researchers traveled to a remote Pacific island to investigate an object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020. They said the object is likely trees, not the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane.
author: BBC World

title: World Food Programme cuts Gaza aid, serving 1.1 million people
content: Funding shortages are prompting the World Food Programme to cut its assistance in Gaza. The UN agency’s reach in the Palestinian territory will decline by roughly one‑third, dropping the number of people served from 1.6 million to about 1.1 million.
summary: The number of people helped by the UN agency in the Palestinian territory will drop by about a third - from 1.6 million to 1.1 million.
author: BBC World

title: Ben Simmons to miss season after tearing right Achilles in Kings practice
content:
Ben Simmons’ attempt to return to the NBA has been halted after he tore his right Achilles tendon during a live drill in a Sacramento Kings practice. Scans confirmed the injury, and the 30‑year‑old will undergo surgery and miss the entire upcoming season. The injury occurred three days before Sacramento’s season opener against the Los Angeles Clippers.

Simmons, a former No. 1 draft pick and three‑time All‑Star, signed a one‑year contract with the Kings in an effort to revive his career. The Achilles tear adds to a five‑year span in which he has faced multiple significant injuries and mental‑health concerns, marking another major setback to his comeback plans.
summary: Ben Simmons, a 30-year-old former No. 1 draft pick who signed a one-year deal with the Sacramento Kings, tore his right Achilles tendon during a live drill at practice. He will undergo surgery and miss the entire season.
author: Guardian Sport

content: President Trump defended his decision to waive Russian sanctions in a Sunday post on Truth Social. He said the move keeps Moscow at the negotiating table, a stance that drew criticism from both sides of the aisle.

title: COP17 biodiversity summit in Yerevan assesses progress on 23 COP15 targets
content:
The UN’s biodiversity summit, held this month in Yerevan, Armenia, is focused on urging governments to meet the 23 targets that were agreed at Cop15 in 2022. The event brings together nearly every country on Earth to address the urgent question of how to curb the rapid destruction of the natural world.  

The summit highlights that human activity is driving this decline, yet no definitive solution has been found to halt it. In late 2022, governments reached an ambitious once‑in‑a‑decade agreement to strengthen nature protection amid scientific warnings that the planet is experiencing the largest loss of life since the extinction of the dinosaurs.  

Today, participants are assessing their progress on those targets for the first time.
summary: The COP17 biodiversity summit is being held this month in Yerevan, Armenia, to push governments to meet the 23 targets agreed at COP15 in 2022. Nearly every country will convene to assess progress on those targets and discuss how to halt the rapid destruction of the natural world.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Marginalization, no primary care raise early death risk in de novo metastatic breast cancer
content: Research published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal reports that individuals who are marginalized or who do not have a primary‑care provider face a higher risk of early death after a diagnosis of de novo metastatic breast cancer. The study links lack of primary‑care access and social marginalization directly to poorer survival outcomes in this patient group.
summary: People who are marginalized have a greater risk of early death from newly diagnosed (de novo) metastatic breast cancer. Lack of access to a primary care provider also increases that early‑death risk, according to research published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Grand Theft Auto VI lets players date characters, prompting criticism
content: Grand Theft Auto VI includes a feature that allows players to build and nurture a romantic relationship with a fictional character. Some observers have expressed that dating a video‑game character crosses a line, describing it as “a step too far.”
summary: Grand Theft Auto VI includes a feature that lets players build and nurture a romantic relationship with a fictional character. Some observers say dating a video game character is a step too far.

content: Antisocial behaviour on buses in England could lead to fines while a new campaign is also being launched for trains. A national campaign asking rail passengers "share the carriage, not the noise" is being launched.
summary: Antisocial behaviour on buses in England could lead to fines of £100. A national campaign asking rail passengers to “share the carriage, not the noise” is being launched.
